papers.title: A GLIMPSE of Dark Matter: JWST Constraints on Early Structure Formation
papers.authors: Julian B. Muñoz, John Chisholm, Seiji Fujimoto, Tiger Yu-Yang Hsiao, Kristen B. W. McQuinn, Priyamvada Natarajan, A. Saldana-Lopez, Hakim Atek, Arghyadeep Basu, Danielle Berg, Ryan Endsley, Lukas J. Furtak, Damien Korber, Rohan P. Naidu, Richard Pan, Daniel Schaerer
papers.abstract: While we have a solid understanding of how dark matter (DM) behaves during recombination ($z\sim 10^3$) and in the late universe ($z\lesssim$ a few), much less is known about intermediate times, when the first galaxies formed. These galaxies provide a powerful handle on DM through structure formation, as halos have to exist to host luminous sources. Here we use recent determinations of the UV luminosity function from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) GLIMPSE lensing program, along with legacy Hubble and Subaru data, to test the small-scale behavior of DM during the epoch of reionization ($z\sim 7$). Marginalizing over astrophysical uncertainties, we find the matter power spectrum to be consistent with the cold-DM prediction down to sub-Mpc scales, with 1$\sigma$ uncertainties of 0.2 dex at $k=3-9 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$ and 0.5 dex at $k=9-27 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$, the smallest scales probed at these early times. For thermal-relic warm DM we constrain $m_{\rm WDM} > 3.2\, \rm keV$ (95% CL), independent of lower-$z$ probes. Our results test small-scale structure formation in a new redshift window and demonstrate the promise of JWST to constrain the nature of DM.

conclusions: In a model-agnostic binned reconstruction, the linear matter power spectrum at $z \sim 4\text{--}8$ agrees with standard $\Lambda$CDM down to sub-Mpc scales, with $1\sigma$ uncertainties on the power amplitude of $\sim 0.17\text{ dex}$ ($\approx 40\%$) at $k = 3\text{--}9\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ and $\sim 0.45\text{ dex}$ (factor of $\sim 3$) at $k = 9\text{--}27\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$.

For thermal-relic warm dark matter, free-streaming suppression of low-mass halos is constrained to $m_{\text{WDM}} > 3.2\,\text{keV}$ (95% CL) after marginalizing over astrophysical feedback and HMF window-function uncertainties—the tightest constraint to date from the epoch of reionization ($z \sim 7$).

Because the observed UVLF continues to rise steeply down to $M_{\text{UV}} \sim -12$, any astrophysical turnover in the star-formation efficiency is bounded by $M_{\text{turn}} \leq 10^{8.4}\,M_\odot$ (95% CL), limiting how strongly reionization and supernova feedback can shut down star formation in early dwarf halos.

The authors note that a major remaining theoretical bottleneck is the lack of converged beyond-CDM $N$-body halo mass functions at $z \sim 5\text{--}10$, which currently has to be parameterized via sharp-$k$ window function parameters.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful context on small-scale power spectrum constraints and explicitly highlights the need for high-redshift beyond-CDM simulations to calibrate the halo mass function, though it focuses on high-$z$ UV luminosity functions and warm dark matter rather than late-time LSS, modified gravity, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Testing dark matter on sub-megaparsec scales ($k \gtrsim 3\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$) is usually done in the late universe using Milky Way satellites, strong lensing, or the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, where billions of years of non-linear evolution and baryonic feedback complicate the picture. Probing these same comoving scales during the epoch of reionization ($z \sim 4\text{--}8$) accesses fluctuations when they were much closer to the linear regime and hosted the very first dwarf galaxies ($M_h \sim 10^9\,M_\odot$). The authors use the ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF—the comoving number density of star-forming galaxies as a function of UV brightness) from the ultra-deep JWST GLIMPSE cluster-lensing survey, combined with HST UVLFs and Subaru/HSC galaxy clustering, to count the smallest star-forming halos down to magnitudes $M_{\text{UV}} \sim -12$. By linking the halo mass function (computed via a sharp-$k$ window function calibrated for non-CDM models) to an empirical halo-galaxy model that marginalizes over star-formation efficiency, dust, and stochastic "bursty" star formation, they reconstruct the small-scale matter power spectrum $P(k)$ and constrain thermal-relic warm dark matter (WDM). This provides an independent high-redshift confirmation that small-scale structure grows as predicted by cold dark matter (CDM) just 750 Myr after the Big Bang.

papers.title: Disentangling constraints on $S_8$ from the high and low redshift CMB
papers.authors: Joann Jones, Ualype de Andrade Uchôa, Scott Dodelson
papers.abstract: The clustering of matter in the universe is quantified by $\sigma_8$, the RMS fluctuations today in linear theory in spheres of radius $8h^{-1}$ Mpc, where $h$ parametrizes the Hubble constant. Surveys of gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering best constrain $S_8\equiv (\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.5} \sigma_8$, where $\Omega_m$ is the energy density of matter in units of the critical density. Comparing this late time measurement to the value of $S_8$ inferred from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), one can test the $\Lambda$CDM prediction for the growth of clustering from the primordial universe to now. Several analyses report hints that CMB measurements of $S_8$ are larger than those from galaxy surveys. However, CMB measurements have information from both high and low redshift due to lensing, and these tests traditionally conflate the two. Here, we present a technique to extract constraints on the cosmological parameters from each redshift component separately, enabling a high-z vs. low-z clustering comparison that was not previously possible. We marginalize over lensing information using a principal component analysis, and show that the primordial CMB from combined Planck 2018, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 prefers $S_8= 0.795\pm0.022$, in agreement with the recent determination from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) of $S_8=0.789\pm0.012$. The clustering inferred from CMB lensing is larger. However, both the level of excess lensing and increase in agreement with DES depends on the prior on the sum of neutrino masses, $\sum m_\nu$. We find that removing lensing brings the CMB towards agreement with DES in any case.

conclusions: With a broad neutrino mass prior ($0.06 < \sum m_\nu < 0.6\,\text{eV}$), the unlensed primordial CMB ($z_* \simeq 1100$) yields $S_8^{z_*} = 0.795 \pm 0.022$, which agrees to within $0.3\sigma$ with the low-redshift DES Year 6 $3\times 2\text{pt}$ measurement ($S_8^{\text{GS}} = 0.789 \pm 0.012$ at $0.3 < z < 1$).

CMB lensing from the 4-point reconstruction alone ($0.7 < z < 5$) prefers a higher clustering amplitude of $S_8^{4\text{-pt}} = 0.836 \pm 0.033$ (or $S_8^{\text{CMBL}} \equiv \sigma_8(\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.25} = 0.814 \pm 0.012$), which pulls the full lensed CMB 2-point constraint up to $S_8 = 0.836 \pm 0.013$ (a $2.6\sigma$ discrepancy with DES Y6).

Both the 2-point peak smoothing and 4-point lensing reconstruction show consistent $>2\sigma$ excesses in the primary lensing principal component $\Theta^{(1)}$ relative to the $\Lambda$CDM prediction from the unlensed CMB ($2.4\sigma$ and $2.2\sigma$, respectively).

The interpretation of these discrepancies depends strongly on the neutrino mass prior: tightening the prior to $\sum m_\nu < 0.1\,\text{eV}$ reduces neutrino suppression of structure growth, raising the unlensed CMB prediction to $S_8^{z_*} = 0.822 \pm 0.018$—which resolves the excess CMB lensing tension (down to $0.4\sigma$–$1.4\sigma$) while only modestly increasing the difference with DES Y6 to $1.3\sigma$.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the $S_8$ tension and structure growth across redshifts by separating early-time recombination constraints from intermediate-redshift CMB lensing, which is central context for testing beyond-$\Lambda$CDM growth with surveys like Euclid.
ai.summary: The $S_8$ tension—where galaxy weak lensing surveys measure weaker late-time matter clustering ($S_8 \equiv \sigma_8 (\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.5}$) than predicted by the cosmic microwave background (CMB)—is usually framed as a discrepancy between early-universe ($z_* \simeq 1100$) and late-universe ($z \lesssim 1$) physics. However, standard CMB temperature and polarization power spectra (2-point functions) are gravitationally lensed by matter along the line of sight at intermediate redshifts ($0.7 < z < 5$, peaking at $z \sim 2$), which smooths the acoustic peaks and mixes low-redshift clustering information into the supposedly primordial CMB constraint. The authors cleanly separate the primordial ($z_*$) and lensing ($z^{\text{CMBL}}$) contributions in combined Planck 2018, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data by decomposing the lensing potential power spectrum $C_L^{\Phi\Phi}$ into principal components (PCs) and marginalizing over the peak-smoothing modes, while separately extracting intermediate-redshift clustering from the 4-point lensing reconstruction. Thanks to the high angular resolution of ACT and SPT-3G, shifts in standard $\Lambda$CDM parameters cannot mimic the oscillatory lensing smoothing pattern (leaving only a 2–3% overlap), making it possible to isolate pure recombination-era predictions and pinpoint whether the $S_8$ tension arises between early and late times or between intermediate-redshift CMB lensing and other probes.

papers.title: The Redshift-Space Cluster-Galaxy Cross-Correlation as a Probe of Gravity on Cosmic Scales
papers.authors: Nicole Marcelina Gountanis, David H. Weinberg, Andrés N. Salcedo, Claire Lamman
papers.abstract: Testing General Relativity (GR) on cosmological scales requires probes that are directly sensitive to gravitational dynamics. We present a Fisher matrix forecast of how well the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) can constrain departures from GR through the cluster infall velocity field, using the redshift-space cluster-galaxy cross-correlation function $\xi^{\rm s}_{\rm cg}(r_p, r_\pi)$ as the primary observable. We construct mock catalogs from the AbacusSummit N-body simulations, using a Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) model for galaxies and a log-normal mass-observable relation for cluster selection. We parameterize departures from GR with a single multiplicative factor $F_{\rm G}$ that rescales halo infall velocities relative to the GR prediction. Marginalizing over the HOD, mass-observable, and cosmological parameters, we find that DESI BGS can constrain $F_{\rm G}$ to $\sigma(F_{\rm G}) = 0.033$ at $z \sim 0.3$. This precision is sufficient to distinguish representative $f(R)$ and Galileon gravity models from GR at $\gtrsim 4\sigma$. The strongest limitation is a degeneracy between $F_{\rm G}$ and the scatter in the cluster mass-observable relation, while the constraint shows no strong degeneracy with any individual HOD parameter. Perfect knowledge of the galaxy-halo connection would improve the constraint to $\sigma(F_{\rm G}) \approx 0.015$, and including the galaxy autocorrelation function in the data vector could recover part of this improvement. The same data vector yields tight constraints on the cosmological parameters, $\sigma(\Omega_m) = 0.010$ and $\sigma(\sigma_8) = 0.010$, only moderately correlated with $F_{\rm G}$. These results demonstrate the potential of DESI BGS cluster-galaxy correlations to test gravity on quasi-linear scales, complementary to existing modified gravity probes and to weak-lensing cluster mass profiles.

conclusions: DESI BGS ($0.25 < z < 0.35$) can constrain the velocity-scaling parameter $F_{\rm G}$ to $\sigma(F_{\rm G}) = 0.033$ (a $3.3\%$ measurement of the infall velocity amplitude), improving over previous SDSS constraints by nearly an order of magnitude and allowing typical $f(R)$ and Galileon models ($F_{\rm G} \approx 1.1\text{--}1.3$) to be distinguished from GR at $\gtrsim 4\sigma$.

The $F_{\rm G}$ constraint is largely immune to degeneracies with galaxy HOD and velocity-bias parameters, with the primary limiting factor being the degeneracy with the cluster mass–observable scatter $\sigma_{\log M_{\rm c}}$ (fixing this scatter improves $\sigma(F_{\rm G})$ by $\sim 23\%$, while perfectly knowing the full galaxy–halo connection lowers it to $\approx 0.015$).

The same cluster–galaxy cross-correlation data vector tightly constrains background and growth parameters to $\sigma(\Omega_m) = 0.010$ and $\sigma(\sigma_8) = 0.010$ from distinct spatial and anisotropic clustering signatures, with only moderate correlation with $F_{\rm G}$.

Directly modeling the full 2D correlation function $\log \xi_{\rm cg}^{\rm s}(r_p, r_\pi)$ captures nearly all the velocity information of the 1D radial infall profile while simultaneously breaking degeneracies with astrophysical nuisance parameters.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly targets tests of screened modified gravity ($f(R)$, Galileon) on quasi-linear scales using $N$-body simulations and motivates building emulators for cluster-galaxy cross-correlations in modified gravity.
ai.summary: In viable modified gravity theories like $f(R)$ or Galileon models, screening mechanisms suppress fifth forces inside high-density virialized cluster cores, but screening weakens in the surrounding quasi-linear infall regions, boosting the velocities of galaxies falling toward the cluster by $10\text{--}30\%$ compared to General Relativity (GR). Because peculiar velocities distort galaxy positions along the line of sight in spectroscopic surveys—creating small-scale "Finger-of-God" elongation and larger-scale coherent squashing/caustics—this infall velocity field is encoded in the 2D redshift-space cluster–galaxy cross-correlation function, $\xi_{\rm cg}^{\rm s}(r_p, r_\pi)$. The authors perform a simulation-based Fisher matrix forecast using the AbacusSummit $N$-body suite at $z=0.3$ to test how well the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) can constrain a phenomenological velocity-rescaling parameter $F_{\rm G}$ (where $F_{\rm G}=1$ is GR), while simultaneously marginalizing over Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) parameters, velocity bias, cluster mass–observable scatter, $\Omega_m$, and $\sigma_8$. This provides a concrete roadmap for testing gravity in the unscreened infall regime and enables a cluster-scale gravitational slip test when combined with weak lensing.

papers.title: Probing Cosmology with Diffusion Models: Memorization, Generalization, and Parameter Estimation
papers.authors: Jiaming Pan, Nicholas Kern
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive cosmological simulations, but simple metrics like reconstruction fidelity do not guarantee a surrogate can be trusted for scientific inference. To explore this, we train diffusion models on HI fields from the CAMELS IllustrisTNG simulations and test how three properties change with training-set size: memorization of individual training examples, agreement with one- and two-point statistics (the pixel-value distribution and the power spectrum), and estimation of cosmological parameters from the generated fields. At fixed model size, generative models trained with smaller, less diverse training data produced memorized samples. While this is a well known phenomenon, we show that this leads to miscalibrated parameter densities for cosmological inference tasks. At fixed size, there is a training set size with enough information content to enable a model to generalize, at which point posterior density estimation with neural surrogates can be well-calibrated. We demonstrate that a neural surrogate can therefore pass visual, one-point and power-spectrum convergence tests while still resulting in overconfident parameter estimation in a cosmological inference pipeline. Thus, tests of model generalization should be an additional check for inference pipelines adopting neural surrogates.

conclusions: A diffusion model trained on a small dataset ($N_{\rm 2D} = 2^6$ to $2^8$ slices) almost entirely memorizes its training images (median pixel cosine similarity $> 0.994$), yet still accurately reproduces the true 1-point pixel histogram and 2D power spectrum—showing that standard summary-statistic checks cannot detect memorization.

Because a memorized model outputs nearly identical fields regardless of the initial random noise seed, using it for parameter inference yields confidence intervals for $\Omega_m$ that are $\sim 2.5\times$ narrower than ground truth (covering only 9/32 and 16/32 of held-out cosmologies at nominal 68% and 95% confidence, compared to 27/32 and 32/32 for real simulation slices).

As training set size increases, models undergo a sharp transition from memorization to generalization at a critical dataset size that scales with neural network capacity (e.g., jumping from a sample novelty fraction $G=0.34$ at $N_{\rm 2D}=512$ to $G=1.0$ at $N_{\rm 2D}=1024$ for UNet-128, while the larger UNet-256 only reaches $G=0.84$ at $N_{\rm 2D}=1024$).

Right at the memorization-to-generalization transition ($N_{\rm 2D} = 2^{10}$), summary statistics temporarily degrade (losing $\sim 1/3$ of large-scale power and high-density tail pixels), before recovering both accurate power spectra and well-calibrated 68% posterior coverage (24–25 out of 32 test cosmologies) once well into the generalized regime ($N_{\rm 2D} \ge 2^{12}$).
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the validation, training-set sizing, and statistical calibration of machine-learning emulators and field-level cosmological surrogates, which is a key methodological area in your profile.
ai.summary: Generative AI models—specifically diffusion models, which learn to generate complex images by iteratively removing noise—are increasingly used as fast field-level emulators for expensive cosmological simulations. However, if a neural network is trained on too few simulations relative to its size, it can simply memorize the training maps rather than learning the underlying physics needed to generate genuinely new realizations. To investigate how this affects cosmological parameter inference, the authors train conditional attention-UNet diffusion models of varying capacities on $2^6$ to $2^{15}$ 2D neutral hydrogen ($\mathrm{H\,I}$) maps from the CAMELS IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical suite, conditioned on $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$. They evaluate the generated fields using three criteria: feature-space similarity to the training set (to detect memorization), 1-point pixel histograms and 2-point power spectra, and posterior calibration when inferring $\Omega_m$ via a separate neural regressor. Crucially, they show that a memorized diffusion emulator can pass visual inspections as well as 1-point and power-spectrum tests with flying colors, yet produce severely under-dispersed, overconfident parameter posteriors because different random seeds collapse onto the same memorized training fields.

papers.title: Early Dark Energy Crowds Out Interacting Dark Energy
papers.authors: William Giarè, Jeremy Sakstein
papers.abstract: We investigate whether interacting dark energy can provide additional relief to the Hubble tension once early dark energy (EDE) is present. Considering a cosmology containing EDE, an independent late-time dark energy fluid with an equation of state fixed at $w\simeq-1$ interacting with cold dark matter, and a cosmological constant, we find that the data strongly drive the model toward the non-interacting limit. The best fit effectively reduces to the standard EDE cosmology, where a non-zero EDE component provides most of the required increase in $H_0$, leaving little statistical gain for the interaction. Although energy transfer from dark matter to dark energy can raise $H_0$ further, this limited gain is rapidly outweighed by the deterioration of the fit to low-redshift observations. In particular, since the CMB tightly constrains the early-time physical matter density, any additional energy transfer requires a lower present-day matter abundance. Such low values are strongly disfavored by Type Ia supernovae. We show that this limitation becomes particularly severe once EDE has already raised $H_0$ and that the same mechanism extends to a broad class of post-recombination interactions. Allowing a dynamical dark energy equation of state of the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder form does not alter our conclusions.

conclusions: In a joint fit to CMB (Planck + ACT DR6 + SPT-3G), DESI BAO, DES-Dovekie SNe Ia, and SH0ES, the best-fit model collapses to the non-interacting EDE-only limit ($\xi = -3.5 \times 10^{-4}$, $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm tot} = -0.02$), yielding $H_0 = 71.51 \pm 0.71\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ ($70.88\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ at best fit) and restricting the interaction-induced matter density shift to $\Delta\Omega_m^{\rm IDE} < 0.0217$ (95% CL).

Once EDE raises $H_0$, only a small statistical reward remains from the SH0ES prior ($\Delta\chi^2 \simeq -4$), which is rapidly outweighed by a severe degradation in the fit to SNe Ia data ($\Delta\chi^2 \simeq +11$ for even modest interactions).

Physically, because the CMB fixes the early-time physical matter density $\omega_{m,\rm early}^{\rm eff}$, transferring energy from CDM to dark energy lowers the present-day matter fraction $\Omega_{m,0}$—an effect compounded by the higher $H_0$ from EDE—pushing $\Omega_{m,0}$ below the range permitted by supernovae.

Allowing the interacting fluid's equation of state to evolve via a $w_0w_a$ (CPL) parametrization does not rescue the interaction ($\Delta\chi^2_{\rm tot} = -2.37$ vs. $-2.41$ without interaction), because perturbative stability restricts this energy-transfer branch to the non-phantom regime ($w(a) \geq -1$), whereas the DESI-preferred phantom-crossing solution ($w_0 = -0.84, w_a = -0.55$, $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm tot} = -8.88$) actually lowers $H_0$ to $70.33\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly investigates dynamical and interacting dark energy extensions, the Hubble tension, and cosmological likelihood combinations of Planck/ACT/SPT CMB, DESI BAO, and DES 5-year SNe Ia.
ai.summary: Proposed solutions to the Hubble tension typically rely on either early-time new physics like Early Dark Energy (EDE)—a scalar field that briefly boosts the pre-recombination expansion rate to shrink the sound horizon—or late-time mechanisms like Interacting Dark Energy (IDE), where cold dark matter transfers energy to dark energy. Because DESI BAO and supernova data recently hinted at non-standard late-time dark energy dynamics, it is natural to ask whether combining EDE with late-time IDE can work together to fully resolve the $H_0$ tension. The authors test a hybrid model containing an axion-like EDE scalar field, a cosmological constant $\Lambda$, and an independent dark energy fluid exchanging energy with cold dark matter ($Q_c^\nu = \xi H \rho_{\rm fld} u_c^\nu$) against CMB (Planck, ACT DR6, SPT-3G), DESI BAO, recalibrated DES 5-year supernovae (DES-Dovekie), and SH0ES data, using both MCMC sampling and profile likelihoods. They find that EDE effectively "crowds out" the interacting dark sector: because the CMB tightly anchors the early-time physical matter density, decaying dark matter into dark energy alongside an EDE-boosted $H_0$ forces the present-day matter fraction $\Omega_{m,0}$ to drop to values strongly disfavored by Type Ia supernovae.

papers.title: Core-collapse universality for inelastic self-interacting dark matter halos
papers.authors: Evan Batteas, Alexander Brisebois, Maheen Hemani, Maximilian Heyne, J. Leo Kim, Lukas Lehmann, Laura Sagunski, Aster Schnell, Sean Tulin
papers.abstract: We study the gravothermal collapse of inelastic dark matter halos with velocity-dependent elastic and dissipative self-interactions. Within the gravothermal fluid framework, we derive the effective cooling rate for dark matter upscattering to an excited state followed by decay back to the ground state, with emitted states carrying off energy from the halo. We solve the gravothermal fluid equations numerically to simulate spherically symmetric halos over the core-growing and collapse phases of their evolution. While halos with purely elastic self-interactions have universal evolution trajectories, inelastic dark matter halos exhibit much more diversity in their evolution. Nevertheless, inelastic halo dynamics contain a hidden parametric universality from which we derive a semi-analytic formula for calculating the halo collapse time for arbitrary velocity-dependent elastic and inelastic cross sections without the need for simulations.

conclusions: Derived the first-principles effective cooling rate $\Gamma_{\rm cool}$ for velocity-dependent inelastic SIDM from the two-state Boltzmann equations, correcting an overcounting factor of 2 in earlier literature.

Found that varying the mass splitting $\delta$ non-monotonically alters halo core-collapse times: collapse is maximally accelerated when the loss velocity $\nu_{\rm loss} = \sqrt{2\delta/m_1}$ matches the halo's typical velocity dispersion, but becomes severely delayed at large $\delta$ due to Boltzmann suppression of upscattering and loop-level suppression of elastic scattering.

Established a "hidden" parametric universality controlled by a single cooling-strength parameter $\xi$, allowing the total collapse rate to be modeled semi-analytically as $t_{\rm coll}^{-1} = (A\tau_{\rm el})^{-1} + (B\tau_{\rm cool})^{-1}$.

Calibrated this semi-analytic formula against an ensemble of gravothermal simulations, reproducing halo collapse times to within $\mathcal{O}(10\%)$ across more than three orders of magnitude without needing new simulations.
ai.relevance_reason: While this paper develops a fast semi-analytic surrogate to bypass expensive dark matter simulations, it focuses on galactic-scale dissipative dark matter halo profiles rather than cosmological large-scale structure, modified gravity, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In standard cold dark matter (CDM), particles only interact via gravity, whereas self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) allows particles to scatter off one another—redistributing heat to flatten central halo "cusps" into constant-density cores, and eventually triggering a runaway central density spike known as gravothermal core-collapse. This paper investigates dissipative SIDM (dSIDM), where colliding ground-state dark matter particles upscatter into a slightly heavier excited state (separated by a mass splitting $\delta$) and promptly decay back down by emitting light hidden-sector states that escape the halo and carry away kinetic energy. Using the gravothermal fluid approximation—which models the dark matter halo as a spherically symmetric, heat-conducting self-gravitating gas rather than running costly $N$-body simulations—the authors derive the effective radiative cooling rate from the two-fluid Boltzmann equations and simulate halo evolution across velocity-dependent elastic and inelastic cross sections. Because dissipative cooling breaks the well-known universal evolution trajectory of purely elastic SIDM halos, the authors uncover a hidden parametric universality that enables them to write down an accurate semi-analytic formula for the halo collapse time directly from particle physics parameters, completely bypassing the need to run numerical simulations for every model point.

papers.title: Simulating and Characterizing Non-Gaussian Small-Scale Polarized Emission
papers.authors: Mark A. Bishop, Brandon S. Hensley, Krzysztof M. Gorski, Charles Lawrence, Graça Rocha
papers.abstract: Galactic foregrounds present a major challenge for cosmic microwave background (CMB) cosmology as their amplitudes exceed the target primordial $B$-mode signal. While small-scale interstellar medium (ISM) emission is expected to be highly complex, current foreground simulations cannot reproduce the filamentary, non-Gaussian features of ISM structure in a stochastic way. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for generating stochastic small-scale foreground emission, using polarized synchrotron observations as an example use case. This method is capable of producing many independent realizations that additionally inherit morphological information from large angular scales. The underlying structural complexity incorporates anisotropic, multifractal, and advected non-Gaussian features that are tunable with a small number of parameters that carry physical interpretations. Because standard power spectra do not describe the complex phase coherence required for the structural complexity, we evaluate the synthetic fields using higher-order statistics, demonstrating that the Minkowski functionals and structure functions partially capture varying degrees of non-Gaussianity. This work lays the necessary foundation for new foreground simulation suites with stochastic realizations of possible non-Gaussian structure.

conclusions: Realistic small-scale ISM foregrounds can be stochastically synthesized using three key ingredients: harmonic-space coordinate transformations ($\mathbb{G}$, parameterized by stretch $s_\ell, s_m$ and orientation $\theta_0$) for directional anisotropy, log-normal cascades ($\lambda \in (0,1)$) for heavy-tailed multifractal intermittency, and multiscale Lagrangian advection ($c$, representing eddy turnover times) for phase-coherent filaments.

Minkowski functionals (topological/geometrical descriptors of excursion sets) capture the heavy-tailed non-Gaussianity introduced by the multifractal parameter $\lambda$, but are largely insensitive to global directional anisotropies and the phase coherence created by Lagrangian advection.

Structure functions (higher-order moments of scale-dependent spatial increments) isolate full-sky directional anisotropies and measure multifractal intermittency via the scaling exponent $\zeta_p$, yet average out localized phase information when integrated over the full sky, making them blind to advected filamentary structures.

Integrating this pipeline with the `PySM` (`s6`) synchrotron framework produces realistic 23 GHz full-sky polarization maps ($Q, U$) that preserve WMAP large-scale morphology ($\ell \lesssim 50$) and match the standard isotropic model's small-scale power spectrum ($\ell \gtrsim 50$) outside a $f_{\mathrm{sky}} = 60\%$ Galactic mask, while exhibiting up to $\sim 3\times$ more unmasked small-scale power near the Galactic plane due to anisotropic concentration.
ai.summary: To detect primordial $B$-mode polarization in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)—the curl-like polarization pattern sourced by inflationary gravitational waves—cosmologists must subtract Galactic foregrounds like polarized synchrotron and thermal dust emission, which are orders of magnitude brighter. On small angular scales where full-sky data is lacking, standard foreground simulations (such as the `PySM` Python Sky Model) inject synthetic fluctuations as isotropic, Gaussian random fields, failing to capture the intricate, non-Gaussian filamentary structures driven by magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in the interstellar medium (ISM). To solve this, the authors develop a fast, stochastic synthesis framework that generates realistic small-scale polarized synchrotron realizations anchored to large-scale WMAP observations using three physically tunable steps: warping spherical harmonic coordinates $(\ell, m)$ to create directional anisotropies, applying a multiplicative log-normal cascade to induce multifractal "burstiness" (intermittency), and using multiscale Lagrangian advection to shear clumpy clouds along synthetic velocity streamlines into coherent filaments. Because the standard angular power spectrum $C_\ell$ is blind to phase correlations, the authors benchmark their maps with higher-order statistics, providing a crucial tool for stress-testing CMB component-separation pipelines against realistic non-Gaussian foregrounds.

papers.title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
papers.authors: Cullan Howlett, L. Giani, Elizabeth G. O'Brien, A. Whitford, Tamara M. Davis, J. Aguilar, S. Ahlen, U. Andrade, E. Armengaud, S. BenZvi, F. Beutler, D. Bianchi, D. Brooks, R. Gaztañaga, Satya Gontcho A Gontcho, G. Gutierrez, C. Hahn, K. Honscheid, D. Huterer, M. Ishak, S. Juneau, T. Karim, D. Kirkby, A. Kremin, O. Lahav, A. Lambert, C. Lamman, M. Landriau, L. Ravoux, G. Rossi, R. Ruggeri, L. Samushia, E. Sanchez, C. Saulder, E. F. Schlafly, D. Schlegel, M. Schubnell, J. Silber, M. Siudek, G. Tarlé, B. A. Weaver, H. Zou
papers.abstract: We present measurements of the scale of cosmic homogeneity using the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the largest publicly available spectroscopic extragalactic survey to date. Using a counts-in-spheres estimator applied to nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six independent redshift bins spanning $0.1 < z < 2.1$, we measure the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$ and define the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the point at which the galaxy distribution reaches within 1\% of the homogeneous asymptotic value. We find that all tracers clearly transition to homogeneity, with the galaxy homogeneity scale ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}$ $h^{-1}$Mpc depending on the tracer redshift, galaxy bias, and modelling used to extract the scale. Using a cosmology-dependent model, we reconstruct the underlying matter homogeneity scale, finding it decreases monotonically with redshift in excellent agreement with $\Lambda$CDM predictions. We identify a systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ between measurements in the North and South Galactic Caps, largely due to fiber assignment effects reproduced in our simulations. Accounting for this, and with a complementary demonstration using toy models that our methodology correctly identifies inhomogeneous universes in all but rather finely-tuned observer configurations, this hence provides strong evidence in favour of the cosmological principle across our full redshift range. Our matter homogeneity scale measurements are consistent with, and substantially more precise than, previous constraints from WiggleZ and SDSS, demonstrating the power of DESI data for precision tests of the cosmological principle.

conclusions: The galaxy homogeneity scale $R_H$ (where the correlation dimension reaches $D_2 = 2.97$) clearly transitions to homogeneity across all six DESI DR1 tracer bins ($0.1 < z < 2.1$), ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ depending on redshift and galaxy bias.

Reconstructing the underlying dark matter distribution yields a matter homogeneity scale $R_H^{\mathrm{matter}}$ that decreases monotonically with redshift—from $67.7^{+1.1}_{-1.0}\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ at $z_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.295$ down to $40.0^{+0.2}_{-0.2}\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ at $z_{\mathrm{eff}}=1.491$ (NGC)—in tight agreement with $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ gravitational growth predictions.

A systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ in the raw galaxy homogeneity scale between the North and South Galactic Caps is reproduced in AbacusSummit mocks and traced to small-scale fiber assignment incompleteness; it is largely absorbed by bias, shot-noise, and counterterm parameters when reconstructing the matter homogeneity scale.

Tests on inhomogeneous toy models (fractal Swiss-cheese, Gaussian, and $800\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ Giant Void distributions) prove that normalising counts with redshift-shuffled random catalogues still detects large-scale inhomogeneity unless the observer sits precisely at the centre of an isotropic void/overdensity, refuting recent claims that DESI DR1 shows no transition to homogeneity within $400\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$.

ai.summary: A foundational assumption of standard cosmology is the cosmological principle—that the Universe becomes statistically homogeneous and isotropic on sufficiently large scales—which is crucial to test against inhomogeneous models and cosmic backreaction scenarios. To quantify where this transition occurs, the authors analyse nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six redshift bins ($0.1 < z < 2.1$) from DESI Data Release 1 using the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$, which measures the logarithmic slope of the average number of galaxies inside spheres of radius $r$ (normalized by unclustered random catalogues) and approaches $3$ in a uniform distribution. Defining the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the radius where $D_2(r)$ reaches within $1\%$ of $3$ ($D_2 = 2.97$), they combine direct spline fits with perturbation-theory clustering models calibrated on AbacusSummit and EZmock simulations to disentangle galaxy bias and fiber-collision systematics from the underlying dark matter distribution. Furthermore, by testing their pipeline on toy inhomogeneous universes (including fractal and giant-void models), they demonstrate that using random catalogues does not artificially force homogeneity unless an observer sits closely at the centre of a spherical structure, providing the most precise confirmation of the cosmological principle across cosmic time to date.

papers.title: Gravitational Wave Background from Metastable Current-Carrying Cosmic Strings
papers.authors: Ivan Rybak, Rinku Maji, Qaisar Shafi
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) generated by networks of current-carrying metastable cosmic strings (MSCSs). Extending previous studies, we include the possibility of vorton formation phenomenologically. We construct an analytical template that provides a fast and accurate approximation to the spectrum in the frequency range probed by pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). We also show how the parameters of cosmic string networks determine the low-frequency slope. For the frequency range relevant for LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK), we derive an analytical expression that constrains the scale-invariant part of the SGWB. Finally, we confront the model with current constraints from PTAs and the LVK collaboration. We identify regions of the parameter space that can produce a signal consistent with PTA observations but are in tension with LVK constraints, suggesting that additional mechanisms to suppress the high-frequency spectrum are required for a consistent interpretation of the PTA signal

conclusions: The presence of worldsheet currents modifies string loop dynamics, alters the loop-length-to-frequency relation, and opens an energy-loss channel via vector radiation, shifting the characteristic frequencies and suppressing the amplitude of the SGWB.

Two distinct low-frequency scaling regimes emerge naturally: an asymptotic $\Omega_{\mathrm{gw}} \propto f^3$ slope when the cutoff is set by the finite network lifetime, and an intermediate/transient $\Omega_{\mathrm{gw}} \propto f^2$ regime when exponential suppression of the loop distribution dominates.

Vorton formation halts radiation once loops shrink to a stationary size $l_{\mathrm{vort}} = P_{\mathrm{vort}} l_b Y_b$, suppressing the high-frequency tail of the gravitational wave spectrum while leaving the low-frequency PTA regime virtually unchanged.

Fitting the analytical template to NANOGrav 15-year data yields Bayes factors comparable to standard metastable strings, but parameter regions explaining the PTA signal remain in tension with the LVK upper bound ($\Omega_{\mathrm{gw}}(25\,\mathrm{Hz}) < 2.8 \times 10^{-9}$) or cosmological vorton abundance limits, pointing to the need for additional high-frequency suppression mechanisms.
ai.summary: Cosmic strings are one-dimensional topological defects formed during symmetry-breaking phase transitions in the early Universe; if they are "metastable" (eventually decaying via monopole-antimonopole nucleation), their oscillating loops can generate a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) that potentially explains the nanohertz signal recently detected by Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs). While most studies assume simple, featureless strings, realistic high-energy physics models often predict "current-carrying" (or superconducting) strings where additional particle excitations propagate along the string core and can stabilize shrinking loops into stationary rings called vortons. The authors model these networks using a charge-velocity-dependent one-scale (CVOS) framework for chiral (light-like) currents, deriving the loop distribution function and building a fast analytical SGWB template that accounts for electromagnetic vector radiation and vorton formation. They then confront this template with NANOGrav 15-year PTA data and high-frequency LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) bounds to test whether worldsheet currents and vortons can simultaneously explain the nanohertz background and evade high-frequency gravitational wave limits.

papers.title: Machine Learning Based Classification of Type 1 Active Galactic Nuclei
papers.authors: Jie Li, Xu-Liang Fan
papers.abstract: Aims. We aim to provide a machine learning based method to distinguish type 1 quasars and type 1 Seyfert galaxies based on photometric data, which could be applied to large all-sky surveys. The method can also be used to obtain relatively complete samples of Seyfert galaxy candidates when broad-line AGNs have been selected. Results. The results of PCA show that quasars and Seyfert galaxies are partial distinguishable. The supervised classifier based on random forest (RF) achieves good performances for type 1 quasars with a F1 score of 0.967. The performance for classifying Seyfert galaxies is worse, with a F1 score of 0.791. Increasing the classification threshold can help to derive a sample of Seyfert galaxies with high purity. The classifier are then applied to the cross-matched sample with DESI DR1. When compared with the results of spectroscopic classification, quasars also show high precision and recall. For Seyfert galaxies identified by RF classifier, there are plenty of less luminous sources who are classified as quasars by spectroscopic method. If they are regarded as Seyfert galaxies, our classifier also performs well to predict Seyfert galaxies. Both the median SEDs and the fraction of Seyfert galaxies derived by our classifier are similar with those for the training sample, while the fraction of Seyfert galaxies for spectroscopic classification are lower at all redshift. These results indicate that our classifier can recover the features of Seyfert galaxies, at least those similar to the Seyfert galaxies in the training sample.

conclusions: A supervised Random Forest classifier trained on multi-wavelength photometric features separates Type 1 quasars with high accuracy ($F_1 = 0.967$) and Type 1 Seyfert galaxies with moderate accuracy ($F_1 = 0.791$), where increasing the decision threshold boosts the purity of the Seyfert candidate sample.

When applied to a cross-matched DESI DR1 validation dataset, the photometric classifier identifies a substantial population of lower-luminosity AGNs as Seyfert galaxies that automated spectroscopic pipelines label as quasars.

The median spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and redshift-dependent Seyfert fractions predicted by the Random Forest model closely match the training catalog properties, whereas standard spectroscopic classifications systematically under-predict the Seyfert fraction across all redshifts.
ai.summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are supermassive black holes actively accreting matter at the centers of galaxies; "Type 1" AGNs are viewed face-on enough that we see broad emission lines from fast-moving gas near the black hole, and they are traditionally split into lower-luminosity "Seyfert galaxies" (where the host galaxy's starlight is still clearly visible) and ultra-luminous "quasars" (which outshine their hosts). Because separating these two populations usually requires expensive spectroscopic follow-up or arbitrary luminosity cuts, the authors develop a Random Forest machine learning classifier that uses only multi-band photometric data (brightnesses and colors across different wavelength filters) along with Principal Component Analysis (PCA). They train the model on known AGN catalogs and test it on cross-matched data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Data Release 1 (DESI DR1), demonstrating that photometric features alone can reliably assemble clean catalogs of quasars and Seyfert candidates across massive sky surveys.

papers.title: Gravitational Dark Matter Production from Spectator Field in $R^2$-Higgs Inflation
papers.authors: Arnab Samanta, Rajesh Mondal, Tanmoy Modak
papers.abstract: We investigate the cosmological gravitational dark matter production of spectator field $\chi$ in the multifield $R^2$-Higgs inflation. The spectator field $\chi$ couples to gravity only through a non-minimal coupling $\xi_\chi\chi^2R$ and serves as a dark matter (DM) candidate. Working consistently in the Einstein frame, we derive the equation of motion of the background fields and fluctuations at linear order using the doubly covariant formalism. We show the dark matter production and the subsequent comoving relic abundance heavily depend on this effective mass of the field $\chi$. Specifically, we find that there exists cancellation regions in the effective mass-squared of $\chi$, which ensures the correct relic abundance is achieved. Further, we show that the preheating from Higgs and Goldstone may play critical role in accounting the observed relic density.

conclusions: In the Einstein frame, the spectator field's effective mass squared $m_{\mathrm{eff},(\chi)}^2$ receives distinct contributions from the transformed scalar potential, field-space curvature, background evolution, and Ricci curvature; for $0 \le \xi_\chi \lesssim 1/6$, cancellations make $m_{\mathrm{eff},(\chi)}^2 < 0$ during inflation, driving tachyonic exponential amplification of super-horizon modes, whereas $\xi_\chi > 1/6$ prevents any excitation above the vacuum.

For dark matter masses above the Hubble scale at the end of inflation ($m_\chi \gtrsim H_e \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}\,M_{\mathrm{P}}$), the comoving number density $Y_\chi$ freezes out within $\mathcal{N} \sim 1.2$ $e$-folds after inflation—safely before preheating completes and linear perturbation theory breaks down—whereas lighter fields ($m_\chi < H_e$) undergo continued parametric resonance.

The observed dark matter relic density $\Omega_\chi h^2 \simeq 0.12$ is reproduced for superheavy dark matter up to $m_\chi \simeq 5.0\,H_e \simeq 3.5 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for a conformal coupling ($\xi_\chi = 1/6$) and up to $m_\chi \simeq 11.8\,H_e \simeq 8.4 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for minimal coupling ($\xi_\chi = 0$).

Computing Higgs and Goldstone preheating directly from the inflationary parameters yields fixed preheating temperatures of $T_{\mathrm{pre}} \simeq (4.9\text{--}7.2) \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ across the benchmark models, removing reheating temperature as an arbitrary free parameter in the relic abundance prediction.
ai.summary: Even if dark matter has no direct interactions with the Standard Model, it can still be produced purely gravitationally in the early Universe as quantum fluctuations of a "spectator" scalar field (a field that does not drive inflation) are amplified by the rapidly changing spacetime geometry during and shortly after inflation. This paper investigates gravitational dark matter production of a spectator field $\chi$ with a non-minimal coupling $\xi_\chi \chi^2 R$ within multifield $R^2$-Higgs inflation, where inflation is driven jointly by the Higgs boson and a Starobinsky $R^2$ curvature term. Rather than mixing reference frames as in previous approximations, the authors work consistently in the Einstein frame using a doubly covariant formalism (covariant in both spacetime and the curved multifield space) to track how the curved field-space geometry and background fields modify the spectator field's effective mass. They also explicitly model post-inflationary preheating—the rapid, non-perturbative transfer of energy into Higgs and Goldstone bosons—which fixes the reheating temperature from first principles and tightly constrains the dark matter mass and coupling parameter space that yields the observed relic density $\Omega_\chi h^2 \simeq 0.12$.

papers.title: Testing Extended Exponential Infrared Teleparallel Gravity with CMB, DESI, and PantheonPlus
papers.authors: Mahmoud Hashim, Jackson Levi Said, Waleed El Hanafy, Eleonora Di Valentino
papers.abstract: We place cosmological constraints on an extended exponential infrared (EExpIR) $f(T)$ teleparallel gravity model using current observational datasets. The extension is characterized by an additional parameter, $b$, which governs the late-time cosmological dynamics. Owing to the existence of two solution branches, phase-space analysis is employed to select the cosmological branch and to establish an appropriate prior range for the new parameter. In this framework, the torsion sector acts as an effective dark-energy component, exhibiting a smooth evolution from a quintessence-like phase to a phantom regime, while recovering the standard cosmological behavior at early times. To constrain the model parameters, we combine early-Universe observations from Planck, ACT, and SPT measurements of the CMB with late-time probes from DESI BAO and PantheonPlus Type Ia supernovae. Using the full dataset, including the SH0ES calibration, we obtain $b=0.573^{+0.016}_{-0.060}$ and $H_0=70.67^{+0.31}_{-0.35}~{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ at 68\% CL. Model comparison based on Bayesian evidence reveals that the EExpIR $f(T)$ and the $\Lambda$CDM models are statistically indistinguishable when only CMB data are considered, whereas the inclusion of the full cosmological dataset with SH0ES leads to a weak preference in favor of $\Lambda$CDM.

conclusions: A dynamical systems / phase-space analysis of the Lambert-$W$ solution branches shows that the principal branch with $0.5 < b < 1$ is the only one that reproduces standard early-time matter domination before transitioning to a stable late-time accelerated attractor (exhibiting a quintessence-to-phantom crossing in $w_{\rm eff}$).

Combining CMB (Planck, ACT, SPT), DESI DR2 BAO, and SH0ES-calibrated Pantheon+ supernovae constrains the deformation parameter to $b = 0.573^{+0.016}_{-0.060}$ and pushes the inferred Hubble constant up to $H_0 = 70.67^{+0.31}_{-0.35}\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ (at 68% CL), partially easing the Hubble tension compared to $\Lambda$CDM.

At the linear perturbation level, torsional modifications alter the effective gravitational coupling ($Q = 1/f_T$) and generate a non-vanishing gravitational slip on ultra-large scales, producing a slight enhancement of the CMB temperature power spectrum at $\ell \lesssim 5$ while remaining nearly indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM at higher multipoles.

Despite the higher $H_0$, the late-time expansion history is too rigid when tested against low-redshift geometric probes: Bayesian evidence reveals that EExpIR $f(T)$ is statistically indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM using CMB data alone, strongly disfavored by CMB+DESI+Pantheon+ without SH0ES, and weakly disfavored when the SH0ES prior is included.
ai.relevance_reason: Tests a modified gravity model at the background and linear perturbation levels using combined Planck/ACT/SPT CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ likelihoods, directly touching on dynamical effective dark energy and the Hubble tension.
ai.summary: Instead of attributing late-time cosmic acceleration to a cosmological constant $\Lambda$, teleparallel gravity reformulates gravity in terms of spacetime torsion (twisting) rather than curvature, and $f(T)$ theories generalize the torsion scalar $T$ in the action—much like $f(R)$ generalizes the Ricci scalar—so that late-time acceleration emerges geometrically while keeping the field equations second-order. In this paper, the authors study the Extended Exponential Infrared (EExpIR) $f(T) = T \exp[\beta(T_0/T)^b]$ model, which acts like standard General Relativity at high redshift ($T \gg T_0$) but introduces a single extra free parameter $b$ that drives an effective dynamical dark energy component at late times. They first use a dynamical systems phase-space analysis to select the physically viable Lambert-$W$ solution branch and establish priors ($0.5 < b < 1$), then implement both the background and linear perturbation equations (which modify the effective Newton's constant and introduce a difference between the two metric potentials, known as gravitational slip) to constrain the model against combined CMB (Planck, ACT, SPT), DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernova datasets. This provides a clear test of whether infrared torsional modifications can simultaneously fit full CMB angular power spectra and resolve the Hubble tension once low-redshift geometric probes are included.

papers.title: Towards constraining cosmology with HI--galaxy cross-correlations from MeerKLASS
papers.authors: G. Autieri, M. Spinelli, Z. Chen, M. Viel, M. Barberi-Squarotti, P. Bull, S. Camera, I. P. Carucci, S. Cunnington, J. Fonseca, K. Grainge, M. O. Irfan, Y. Li, A. Pourtsidou, M. G. Santos, J. Wang, L. Wolz
papers.abstract: We present an inference of cosmological parameters from the cross-correlation power spectrum between the MeerKLASS 2019 L-band HI intensity maps and the overlapping WiggleZ galaxies at $z \simeq 0.43$. The analysis is intended as a proof of concept to verify that the full pipeline, from the foreground cleaning of the maps to the likelihood analysis, can be applied end-to-end to real data and can return results consistent with the concordance cosmology. The model of the observed power spectrum includes observational effects that are relevant to a single-dish experiment. In the most optimistic scenario in which we hold the astrophysical nuisance parameters fixed, we obtain $H_0 = 65.3^{+5.8}_{-10}\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ and $\Omega_{\text{m}} = 0.44^{+0.12}_{-0.30}$ at the 68% confidence level. We find that sampling the HI amplitude with an informative prior retains most of the constraining power and changes these results by less than 1 sigma. Moreover, using synthetic data, we show that neglecting the observational effects in the model biases the inferred parameters by up to 2.5 sigma and also underestimates their uncertainties. Finally, we show that varying the number of foreground modes removed and the range of scales included changes the inferred parameters by less than 0.5 sigma. These results demonstrate the robustness of our pipeline in modelling HI intensity mapping data, and set the foundation for future cosmological inference with intensity mapping using MeerKLASS and SKAO.

conclusions: Under optimistic assumptions with astrophysical nuisance parameters fixed and a BBN prior, the cross-power spectrum monopole yields $H_0 = 65.3^{+5.8}_{-10}\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$, $\Omega_{\text{m}} = 0.44^{+0.12}_{-0.30}$, and $\sigma_8 = 0.86^{+0.19}_{-0.12}$ ($68\%$ CL), all consistent within $1\sigma$ with Planck 2018 $\Lambda$CDM.

Combining the cross-correlation with Planck 2018 CMB likelihoods constrains the neutral hydrogen abundance to $\Omega_{\text{HI}} = (0.85 \pm 0.17) \times 10^{-3}$, validating the pipeline against prior fixed-cosmology analyses of the same dataset.

Tests on synthetic data show that neglecting observational effects—most notably Cartesian gridding compensation—biases inferred cosmological parameters low by up to $2.5\sigma$ while artificially shrinking the posterior uncertainties.

Varying the number of removed PCA foreground modes ($N_{\text{fg}} = 4, 10, 15$) or applying stricter $(k_\perp, k_\parallel)$ scale cuts shifts the inferred cosmological parameters by less than $0.5\sigma$, though the two lowest-$k$ bins are critical for breaking the $\Omega_{\text{c}}h^2$–$H_0$ degeneracy.
ai.relevance_reason: This paper focuses on 21cm intensity mapping data analysis and linear cross-power spectrum observational systematics, making it loosely related LSS background rather than directly applicable to beyond-ΛCDM simulations, emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Neutral hydrogen (HI) 21cm intensity mapping (IM) surveys large cosmic volumes by measuring the collective radio emission of unresolved gas rather than individual galaxies, but astrophysical foregrounds like Galactic synchrotron emission are four to five orders of magnitude brighter than the cosmological signal. Cross-correlating these radio maps with optical galaxy surveys suppresses foreground residuals and instrumental noise—which do not correlate with galaxy positions—and up to now has mainly been used to measure the HI abundance and bias while holding cosmology fixed. Here, the authors present an end-to-end proof-of-concept cosmological parameter inference using the cross-power spectrum monopole between MeerKLASS L-band single-dish intensity maps and overlapping WiggleZ galaxies at $z \simeq 0.43$. Using the `meer21cm` pipeline and `Cobaya`, they forward-model key observational distortions—including the $1.48^\circ$ telescope beam, principal component analysis (PCA) foreground cleaning signal loss via mock injection transfer functions, Cartesian gridding compensation, and survey window convolution. This work demonstrates that single-dish 21cm IM cross-correlations can be carried all the way to cosmological likelihood inference and establishes essential systematic modelling for upcoming SKAO and MeerKLASS surveys.

papers.title: Probing the local primordial non-Gaussianity with clustering of FRB dispersion measure and galaxies
papers.authors: Indranil Das, Gilbert Holder
papers.abstract: We forecast the sensitivity of a joint fast radio burst (FRB) and galaxy survey to local primordial non-Gaussianity using the full $3\times2$-point statistic: the angular dispersion-measure (DM) auto-spectrum, the DM-galaxy cross-spectrum, and the galaxy auto-spectrum. Local primordial non-Gaussianity imprints a scale-dependent bias on both the free-electron field probed by FRB dispersion measures and the galaxy field. Hence, all three spectra carry information on the local non-Gaussianity amplitude $f_{\rm NL}$. Adopting a DESI-like luminous-red-galaxy sample and an FRB population over 35% of the sky, we forecast $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 5$ for both $N_{\rm FRB} = 10^4$ and $10^5$ at fixed Planck 2018 cosmology, marginalised over three astrophysical bias parameters $(b_e^0, z_{\rm fb}, b_g^{\rm amp})$. The $f_{\rm NL}$ constraint is robust to marginalising over the six $\Lambda$CDM parameters $(\omega_b, \omega_{\rm cdm}, h, A_s, n_s, \tau)$ with Planck priors. At these sample sizes, the galaxy auto-spectrum sets the constraint, while the DM sector's contribution grows with the burst count and becomes decisive for the larger samples anticipated in the SKA era, reaching $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 2$ at $10^7$ bursts.

conclusions: For near-term FRB sample sizes ($N_{\rm FRB} = 10^4$ to $10^5$), the joint $3\times 2$-point analysis yields $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 5$, which is entirely dominated by the galaxy auto-spectrum because the FRB signal is limited by small $(b_e - 1)$ response and host-galaxy DM scatter.

Because DM host noise enters quadratically in the DM auto-covariance but only linearly in the DM-galaxy cross-covariance, the cross-spectrum outperforms the DM auto-spectrum below $N_{\rm FRB} \approx 5\times 10^5$, above which the DM auto-spectrum takes over.

In the SKA era ($N_{\rm FRB} = 10^6$ to $10^7$), the FRB sector surpasses the galaxy-only floor and tightens the joint constraint to $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 3.3$ and $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 2$, respectively—approaching the $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \sim 1$ threshold needed to distinguish multi-field from single-field inflation.

Marginalising over the six $\Lambda$CDM parameters (with Planck priors) leaves $\sigma(f_{\rm NL})$ virtually unchanged, while for $N_{\rm FRB} = 10^6$ the joint probe simultaneously measures galaxy and present-day electron bias amplitudes to $\sim 1\%$–$2\%$ precision and tightens the Planck prior on $h$ by $\sim 20\%$.
ai.relevance_reason: While galaxy bias and $3\times 2$-point LSS statistics are broadly relevant background for Euclid cosmology, this paper focuses on linear-scale primordial non-Gaussianity forecasts with FRBs rather than non-linear modelling, beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Local primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG, parameterised by $f_{\rm NL}$) is a key signature of multi-field inflation that imprints a characteristic $k^{-2}$ scale-dependent bias on large-scale structure tracers, though galaxy survey measurements on ultra-large scales are often limited by observational systematics. Fast radio bursts (FRBs)—millisecond extragalactic radio transients—offer an independent tracer with completely different systematics via their dispersion measure (DM), which integrates the column density of free electrons along the line of sight as radio waves travel through the ionised intergalactic medium. In this paper, the authors perform a tomographic Fisher forecast combining a DESI-like luminous red galaxy (LRG) sample with future FRB surveys over $35\%$ of the sky in a full $3\times 2$-point analysis (galaxy auto-spectrum, DM auto-spectrum, and galaxy-DM cross-spectrum). By modelling the opposing non-Gaussian bias responses of strongly clustered galaxies ($b_g > 1$) and under-biased free electrons ($b_e < 1$), they show how next-generation radio arrays can break astrophysical bias degeneracies and push $f_{\rm NL}$ constraints past the galaxy-only limit.

papers.title: Running cosmological constant in light of recent CMB-BAO data
papers.authors: A. Racioppi, M. Vijar
papers.abstract: We revisit single-field slow-roll inflation driven by a running cosmological constant, i.e. a cosmological constant receiving a logarithmic radiative correction, in light of the latest CMB-BAO data. The relative radiative correction $\delta$ is treated as a free parameter of the model and allowed to be positive or negative. For positive $\delta$, the predictions interpolate between a logarithmic regime and a linear inflation one. Compatibility with CMB-only data is confined to a narrow stripe near the $2\sigma$ border where $\delta$ is relatively large. On the other hand, the predictions fit easily within the constraints including BAO data in a wide range of parameters. For negative $\delta$, the slow-roll approximation breaks down at small field values and the predictions are excluded by data. However, once the effective mass contribution inside the logarithmic correction is taken into account, the negative $\delta$ potential develops a local maximum and behaves like a hilltop model, achieving compatibility with CMB-only data, while agreement with CMB-BAO data is possible only at $2\sigma$.

conclusions: For $\delta > 0$, the inflationary predictions in the $(n_s, r)$ plane interpolate between a pure logarithmic regime ($n_s \to 1 - 1/N_e$, $r \to 0$) and linear inflation, fitting easily within the $1\sigma$ region of the combined CMB+DESI BAO data for $N_e = 50$ e-folds, whereas CMB-only compatibility requires $\delta \gtrsim 0.1$ and sits near the $2\sigma$ boundary.

For an unregularized $\delta < 0$ potential, the slow-roll approximation breaks down near $\phi \to 0$ (requiring a field scale $\phi_0 \gtrsim 15\,M_P$) and predicts a tensor-to-scalar ratio $r \gtrsim 0.07$, which is completely ruled out by current CMB B-mode limits.

Regularizing the $\delta < 0$ potential with an effective mass parameter $0 < \beta < 1$ inside the logarithm turns the model into a hilltop-like potential around $\phi = 0$, restoring $1\sigma$ compatibility with CMB-only data (for $\beta = 0.9, N_e = 60$) while only achieving $2\sigma$ agreement when DESI BAO is included.

In both viable regimes, the inflationary energy scale is $\sim 10^{15}\text{--}10^{16}\text{ GeV}$ and the typical tensor-to-scalar ratio is $r \sim 10^{-2}$, making the scenario testable by upcoming primordial gravitational wave searches with the Simons Observatory and LiteBIRD.
ai.summary: Despite its title, this paper is about early-universe cosmic inflation rather than late-time dark energy: a "running cosmological constant" here refers to an inflaton potential consisting of a constant vacuum energy $\Lambda^4$ modified by a one-loop quantum (Coleman–Weinberg) logarithmic correction, $V(\phi) = \Lambda^4 [1 + \delta \ln(\phi/M)]$. Depending on whether bosons or fermions dominate the quantum loops in the underlying particle physics theory, the relative radiative correction $\delta$ can be positive or negative, which completely changes the shape of the potential. The authors treat $\delta$ as a free effective-field-theory parameter and compute the slow-roll inflationary predictions—specifically the scalar spectral index $n_s$ and tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$—to test the model against recent CMB data (Planck, ACT, SPT, and BICEP/Keck) with and without DESI BAO measurements. Because adding DESI BAO data shifts the preferred $n_s$ toward slightly higher values, it alters which inflationary potentials are favored, and the authors show that the two signs of $\delta$ exhibit a sharp complementarity between the CMB-only and CMB+BAO datasets.

papers.title: Cosmic birefringence tomography with radio galaxies I: Testing birefringence solutions to the CMB-BAO tension
papers.authors: Toshiya Namikawa, Fumihiro Naokawa, Richard Battye, Salvatore Samuele Sirletti
papers.abstract: We present an independent test of cosmic birefringence induced by axionlike particles (ALPs) at low redshift using radio galaxies. We focus on models that can alleviate the mild tension between recent baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements and observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This tension can be explained by a large cosmic birefringence rotation angle generated during the reionization epoch. Such a large rotation can arise if the recent isotropic cosmic birefringence measurements are subject to an $n\pi$ phase ambiguity, with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, or if cold dark matter injects energy into ALPs. We constrain these two scenarios by fitting the cosmic birefringence angles estimated from the jet morphologies and polarization angles of radio galaxies obtained by Battye, Jackson & Browne (2026). For the $n\pi$ model, the radio-galaxy data exclude $|n|\geq 1$ at more than $2\sigma$ for $\log_{10}(m_{\phi}/{\rm eV})\lesssim -30.7$. For the energy injection model, the data are consistent with no energy injection, but with a slight relative preference for a nonzero energy injection compared to the no-injection case. Since our samples are limited to $\sim 3000$ and there could still be several astrophysical uncertainties and statistical fluctuations, further exploration of tomographic cosmic birefringence using a large number of low-redshift radio galaxies is important for independent tests of cosmic birefringence.

conclusions: In the "$n\pi$ phase ambiguity" model, radio-galaxy data rule out nonzero phase shifts ($|n| \ge 1$) at $>2\sigma$ for ultralight ALP masses $\log_{10}(m_\phi / \text{eV}) \lesssim -30.7$, because lighter fields evolve slowly enough to leave an unacceptably large residual polarization rotation of several degrees at $z \le 3$.

papers.title: Cosmological axion-photon interactions with a nonminimal dark gauge sector
papers.authors: Hao Jiao, Dong-Won Jung, Nils A. Nilsson
papers.abstract: We study the cosmological evolution of radiation and dark radiation with nonminimal axion-photon-dark photon couplings. The Chern-Simons-type axion-gauge field interactions between the dark and visible sectors can induce energy conversion between photons and dark photons as well as polarization rotation during the propagation of radiation, leading to CMB spectral distortions and cosmic birefringence. Using the observed CMB monopole spectrum, we constrain the photon-dark photon energy conversion fraction, which is determined by the coupling constants and the evolution of the axion field. We further show that the parity-odd mixing interaction $\phi F\tilde{B}$ can partially relax the constraints on the standard axion-photon coupling, $\phi F\tilde{F}$, derived from the current observational limits of the cosmic birefringence angle.

conclusions: Even though the photon–dark photon conversion fraction $P$ is frequency-independent in the adiabatic regime, exchanging photons between two thermal baths at different temperatures distorts the CMB monopole away from a pure blackbody; COBE/FIRAS data restrict this conversion fraction to $P < 1.39 \times 10^{-4}$ (95% credibility), with a 68% interval of $P = (5.65^{+4.10}_{-3.43}) \times 10^{-5}$.

The observed cosmic birefringence angle $\beta_A$ depends on all three dimensionless coupling combinations $\beta_i = 2g_i(\phi_0 - \phi_{\rm rec})$, meaning the mixed $\phi F\tilde{B}$ portal allows purely dark-sector couplings ($\phi B\tilde{B}$) to alter visible CMB polarization without observing the dark radiation directly.

In the small-coupling regime, the dark-sector correction to the standard birefringence angle is $\langle\beta_A\rangle - \beta_1 \simeq P(\beta_1 - \beta_3)/6$, which is tightly suppressed by the FIRAS spectral distortion bound on $P$ unless the couplings reside near narrow oscillatory minima where net energy conversion returns to zero today.

This paper asks what happens if the dark sector also contains a massless "dark photon" (an unbroken dark $U(1)$ gauge field $B_{\mu\nu}$ forming a thermal dark radiation bath) that couples to the same homogeneous axion dark matter background via mixed ($\phi F\tilde{B}$) and purely dark ($\phi B\tilde{B}$) interactions. By solving the coupled wave equations for visible and dark photons on an expanding FLRW background in the adiabatic approximation, the authors show that the mixed coupling simultaneously rotates photon polarization and converts energy back and forth between the visible and dark radiation baths. Because mixing two blackbodies of different temperatures distorts the Planck spectrum, they use COBE/FIRAS CMB monopole data alongside Planck/ACT cosmic birefringence measurements to jointly constrain the energy conversion fraction and determine how much the dark sector can shift standard bounds on the axion-photon coupling.

papers.title: A deep learning approach to member identification and mass estimation in galaxy clusters
papers.authors: Zicheng Wang, Liping Fu, Wei Du, Wentao Luo, Wenxiang Pei, Zhu Chen, Zhijian Luo, Yicheng Li, Jiachen Qiu, Haoran Zhao, Kaiwen Mai, Weiming Ren
papers.abstract: Accurate dynamical mass estimates of galaxy clusters are essential for studies of cluster formation and evolution and for cosmological applications. However, interloper galaxies, which are not gravitationally bound to the cluster but are incorrectly identified as members, can bias dynamical mass measurements and increase uncertainties. We developed a probabilistic deep-learning framework for cluster member identification and dynamical mass estimation and tested sensitivity to cluster miscentring and radially dependent incompleteness in controlled mock experiments. We used mock galaxy cluster catalogues to train a two-stage model. A long short-term memory (LSTM) network assigns membership probabilities to galaxies arranged by projected phase-space proximity. These probabilities construct membership-weighted projected phase-space density maps, from which a Bayesian neural network (BNN) infers cluster masses and predictive uncertainties. The LSTM membership probabilities are well calibrated and form an isoprobability envelope in projected phase space, with the $\langle p_{\rm mem}\rangle = 0.5$ contour broadly tracing the empirical member--interloper transition. A threshold of $p_{\rm th} = 0.5$ balances member completeness and purity, with high completeness within $R_{\rm proj} < r_{200}$. Membership weighting lowers the residual scatter of the fiducial BNN mass estimator, $\mathrm{BNN}^{\mathrm{Mem}}_{\mathrm{2D}}$, to $\sigma_\epsilon = 0.120$, a 19.5% reduction relative to the unweighted baseline, although predictive uncertainties are not uniformly calibrated across BNN models. Using the brightest cluster galaxy rather than the gravitational centre lowers the median inferred mass by up to 47.6%, with larger reductions at larger centring offsets. By contrast, removing 40% of eligible non-central galaxies within $r_{200}$ lowers it by 6.1% relative to complete catalogues.

Weighting the projected phase-space density map by the inferred membership probabilities reduces the logarithmic mass scatter of the BNN estimator to $\sigma_\epsilon = 0.120\,\text{dex}$, a $19.5\%$ improvement over the unweighted baseline, though predictive uncertainties are not uniformly well-calibrated across model variants.

Interestingly, randomizing the galaxy sequence order yields similar performance to the nearest-neighbour phase-space ordering, suggesting the bidirectional LSTM relies more on individual galaxy features and global context than strict local sequential adjacency.

The inferred dynamical masses are highly sensitive to cluster miscentring—using an offset brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) rather than the true gravitational potential minimum underestimates the median mass by up to $47.6\%$—whereas removing $40\%$ of galaxies inside $r_{200}$ to mimic spectroscopic incompleteness only biases the median mass low by $6.1\%$.

papers.title: Low-variance renoising for weak gravitational lensing shear estimation
papers.authors: Xiangchong Li
papers.abstract: The "renoising" noise-bias correction used by Metacalibration and AnaCal adds to every galaxy image an independent noise field with the statistics of the original noise rotated by 90 degrees. The rotated field cancels, to first order in shear, the anisotropy that the shear-response operation induces in the original noise, at the cost of doubling the noise variance. We derive the general condition that an added noise field must satisfy for this cancellation: the distribution of the total noise -- the original noise transformed with the pixel shear-response operator, plus the added noise carrying an assigned shear dependence that we are free to choose -- must be independent of shear to first order. Under this condition the shear response of the renoised ellipticity is estimated from the known realization of the added noise alone. The rotated noise field, which we call rotation renoising, is one solution of the condition and yields the analytical response estimator of AnaCal. We then construct a second solution, spectral renoising, which adds only a small fraction of the original noise variance: for homogeneous Gaussian noise the added field is an independent, scaled-down copy of the image noise, and its assigned shear response is the same field passed through a fixed filter set by the noise power spectrum deconvolved by the point spread function. Image simulations show that spectral renoising keeps the multiplicative shear bias at the $10^{-3}$ level and raises the effective galaxy number density by about 20 per cent at the faint end.

conclusions: General renoising condition: Any added noise field $n$ cancels first-order noise bias in shear response estimation if the probability distribution of the total effective noise—the original noise subjected to the shear-response operator plus the added noise with a freely chosen assigned shear derivative—is independent of shear to first order.

Variance reduction: Spectral renoising requires adding only a small adjustable fraction $\mu \approx 0.1$ of the original noise variance (about $0.14$ in total when including a filler field to symmetrize a $2\%$ PSF anisotropy), compared to the $100\%$ extra noise variance added by standard $90^{\circ}$-rotated noise.

Increased effective galaxy density: By avoiding the noise doubling of standard rotation renoising, spectral renoising recovers lost survey depth, increasing the effective number density of usable lensing galaxies at the faint end ($i = 27$) by $\sim 20\%$, from $28$ to $34\text{ arcmin}^{-2}$.

Instead of adding a full rotated noise copy, spectral renoising adds a scaled-down noise realization (only $\sim 10\%$ of the original variance) and filters it in Fourier space using the shear derivative of the PSF-deconvolved noise power spectrum. Validated on realistic blended image simulations, this technique keeps shear calibration biases within strict Stage-IV survey requirements while recovering the survey depth lost to traditional renoising.

papers.title: Cosmological constraints on extra radiation and early dark energy with lepton asymmetry and varying quark masses
papers.authors: Yo Toda
papers.abstract: We investigate cosmological constraints on extra radiation and axionlike early dark energy (EDE), allowing primordial lepton asymmetry or light-quark-mass variation during big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). We combine Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae, and primordial helium and deuterium measurements. When both extra radiation and lepton asymmetry are allowed, we obtain $N_{\rm eff}=3.27\pm0.16$, $\xi=0.017\pm0.011$, and $H_0=69.24\pm0.92\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. A positive lepton asymmetry compensates the helium increase caused by extra radiation, allowing a higher inferred Hubble constant even with the LBT helium measurement, which agrees with standard BBN. For EDE, primordial-abundance measurements instead restrict the higher baryon densities associated with larger EDE fractions, which reduce the predicted deuterium abundance. Allowing lepton asymmetry does not relax this restriction. In contrast, a positive light-quark-mass variation increases deuterium and compensates this reduction, permitting larger EDE fractions and a higher inferred Hubble constant. The same variation leaves the extra-radiation constraint nearly unchanged. We also find that allowing lepton asymmetry relaxes the 95\% upper limit on the summed neutrino mass from $0.0640\,{\rm eV}$ to $0.0777\,{\rm eV}$ in the extra-radiation model.

Allowing a positive primordial lepton asymmetry ($\xi = 0.017 \pm 0.011$) reduces the neutron-to-proton ratio enough to cancel the helium increase from extra radiation, reopening the parameter space to $N_{\rm eff} = 3.27 \pm 0.16$ and raising $H_0$ to $69.24 \pm 0.92\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ (reducing the SH0ES tension from $5.74\sigma$ to $3.12\sigma$).

In the $N_{\rm eff} + \xi$ model, marginalizing over lepton asymmetry also relaxes the stringent 95% upper bound on the summed neutrino mass $\sum m_\nu$ from $0.0640\,{\rm eV}$ to $0.0777\,{\rm eV}$.

For axionlike EDE, BBN restricts the fraction of early dark energy ($f_{\rm EDE} < 0.0120$ at 68% C.L.) because EDE fits require a higher baryon density $\Omega_b h^2$, which destroys too much primordial deuterium; adding lepton asymmetry does not help ($f_{\rm EDE} < 0.0113$) because $\xi$ is tightly pinned by helium and actually slightly lowers deuterium.

Allowing a slight increase in light-quark masses during BBN ($\delta_q = 0.0072 \pm 0.0044$) alters nuclear binding energies to boost deuterium production, counteracting the higher baryon density in EDE and relaxing the bound to $f_{\rm EDE} < 0.0187$ ($H_0 = 68.85^{+0.33}_{-0.96}\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, a $4.02\sigma$ tension with SH0ES).
