papers.title: Efficient GLS map-making and assessment of $1/f$ noise impact for future CMB satellite missions
papers.authors: Marta Monelli, Guillaume Patanchon, Avinash Anand
papers.abstract: Time-correlated $1/f$ noise is a major source of large-scale contamination in measurements of the polarized cosmic microwave background (CMB) that can limit sensitivity to primordial $B$ modes. Generalized least-squares (GLS) map-making is optimal for stationary Gaussian noise when its covariance is known, but practical implementations rely on approximations to make the computation tractable. In particular, approximating the noise covariance as circulant enables efficient map-making using fast Fourier transform, but introduces artificial edge effects when applied to finite data chunks. We introduce STITCH (STatistical Inpainting for Timeline CHunks), a preprocessing method that mitigates these effects by extending time-ordered data chunks with synthetic samples that make the extended timelines statistically consistent with the assumed circulant noise model. They can then be processed with standard circulant GLS solvers, preserving their computational efficiency while reducing residuals associated with chunk boundaries. Simulations show that STITCH substantially suppresses these edge effects, bringing the resulting noise power spectra close to those obtained when the circulant approximation holds. We demonstrate negligible impact of our procedure on the recovered signal, such as $E\to B$ leakage, even at large scales. Finally, we investigate how temporal $1/f$ noise projects onto angular scales for representative LiteBIRD-, \emph{Planck}-, and PICO-like scanning strategies. Using noise simulations spanning a range of temporal noise parameters, we fit an effective model to the resulting angular noise spectra. These results provide an empirical characterization of the temporal-to-angular noise mapping for the configurations studied and a basis for further investigations of correlated noise in future CMB polarization missions.

The inpainting preprocessing introduces negligible bias into the recovered sky signal (such as $E \to B$ polarization leakage) and adds only a tiny residual to the large-scale $BB$ power spectrum.

Across all tested satellite scanning strategies, the angular knee multipole $\ell_{\mathrm{knee}}$ scales approximately linearly with the temporal knee frequency $f_{\mathrm{knee}}$, though simple scan-speed rescaling does not fully align results across missions due to differences in scan geometry.

Residuals from STITCH are significantly smaller than sub-pixel pointing effects (where observations do not fall at exact pixel centers), which alone can contribute bias up to $\sim 10\%$ of the primordial $B$-mode power at large scales in CMB-only simulations and an order of magnitude more when Galactic foregrounds are included.

However, because real $1/f$ noise is not periodic across chunk boundaries, this approximation introduces severe large-scale artificial residuals in the reconstructed maps. The authors introduce STITCH, a preprocessing algorithm integrated into the BrahMap framework that appends a short synthetic extension (~16 minutes of constrained Gaussian inpainting assigned to discarded auxiliary pixels) to each data chunk, making the timeline genuinely periodic before running the fast FFT-based solver. Using simulations of future and past CMB satellite missions (LiteBIRD, PICO, and Planck), they demonstrate that STITCH eliminates boundary artifacts while preserving computational speed, allowing them to systematically map out how temporal $1/f$ noise translates into angular noise power across different satellite scanning strategies.

papers.title: Dwarf Galaxy Reticulum II's MeerKAT L-Band Observation: Constraining WIMP Dark Matter
papers.authors: Phillip Badenhorst (1), Michael Sarkis (1), Yin-Zhe Ma (1), Wen-Qing Guo (1), Geoff Beck (2), Qiang Yuan (3), Gyula I.G. Jozsa (4), Steven G. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are particularly promising targets for indirect dark matter searches due to their high mass-to-light ratios and low astrophysical foreground contamination. While radio observations have been widely used to constrain WIMP properties in these systems, the resulting limits remain highly sensitive to poorly constrained magnetic field assumptions. Here we utilize L-band ($1.3$--$1.5$ GHz) observations from the MeerKAT array directed towards dwarf galaxy Reticulum II and measure the surface brightness profile across the dwarf galaxy. Combining these measurements with theoretical models of WIMP annihilation and yield 95% confidence level upper limits on the WIMP annihilation cross-section $\langle\sigma v\rangle \lesssim 10^{-26}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for masses $m_\chi \sim 10$-$200$ GeV (with the assumed uniform magnetic field model and diffusion constant). papers.title: Mapping cluster angular momentum with the rotational kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
papers.authors: Jack Y. L. Kwok, Bernardita Ried Guachalla, William R. Coulton, Selim C. Hotinli, Emmanuel Schaan
papers.abstract: Galaxy clusters carry angular momentum. If the intracluster gas rotates coherently, the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect imprints a dipole on the microwave sky centered on the cluster. We show that microwave maps alone can be used to reconstruct a noisy vector field tracing the projected angular momentum of the ionized gas. We present an optimal multifrequency matched filter (MMF) that isolates the rotational kSZ (rkSZ) signal from the much larger miscentered thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect, cosmic microwave, and infrared background contributions, improving on both real-space oriented stacking and matched filtering of maps cleaned with full-sky multifrequency weights. For the rkSZ profile, we introduce a simple model for coherent intracluster gas rotation and validate it against TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1. The model consists of differentially rotating concentric shells with constant equatorial tangential velocity, characterized by a mass- and redshift-indepedent tangential-to-circular velocity ratio of $v_{\rm tan}/V_{c,200c}=0.18$. Using this model, we forecast single-cluster signal-to-noise (SNR) as a function of mass and redshift for Simons Observatory; cross-correlation with an external catalog of rotation proxies yields a cumulative detection SNR. For an idealized mass-limited catalog with perfectly known spin directions, the cumulative SNR of our optimal MMF reaches $\approx 53$, $25$, and $6$ when including all clusters above $\log_{10}(M_{200c}/M_\odot)>14$, 14.5, and 15, respectively. This work provides a practical framework for CMB measurements of intracluster gas rotation, with applications to the rotational contribution to non-thermal pressure in cluster mass calibration, as well as spin alignments and clustering biases.

conclusions: A simple analytical rotation model—treating the intracluster medium as differentially rotating shells with a constant equatorial tangential speed of $v_{\rm tan} \approx 0.18\,V_{c,200c}$ and a simulation-calibrated radial spin-misalignment profile—reproduces the integrated rkSZ signal measured in IllustrisTNG (TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1) for haloes with $M_{200c} \gtrsim 10^{13.5}\,M_\odot$.

Optimal foreground cleaning is strongly mass-dependent: only the most massive clusters ($M_{200c} \gtrsim 10^{14.7}\,M_\odot$) are dominated by miscentered thermal SZ contamination and require explicit tSZ deprojection, whereas lower-mass clusters ($10^{13.7}$–$10^{14.7}\,M_\odot$) are instrument-noise-dominated and carry most of the total statistical weight.

Uniformly deprojecting the thermal SZ signal across a full cluster catalog sacrifices roughly half of the total signal-to-noise ratio compared to the authors' mass-adaptive multifrequency matched filter (MMF).

For Simons Observatory (SO-goal noise over $f_{\rm sky}=0.4$) cross-correlated with an idealized mass-limited catalog of known cluster spin directions, the cumulative detection SNR reaches $\approx 53$, $25$, and $6$ for mass thresholds of $\log_{10}(M_{200c}/M_\odot) > 14$, $14.5$, and $15$, respectively (while an axis-only tensor estimator without spin-sign information yields $\mathrm{SNR} < 1$).

Measuring this signal is challenging because its peak amplitude is only a few $\mu\mathrm{K}$, swamped by instrumental noise, lensed CMB fluctuations, cosmic infrared background (CIB), and the much brighter thermal SZ (tSZ) signal from random thermal electron motions (which can mimic a dipole if the cluster is slightly miscentered). In this paper, the authors construct a simple analytical model of gas rotation in concentric shells—calibrated and validated against the TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1 hydrodynamical simulations—and develop an optimal linear multifrequency matched filter (MMF) to reconstruct a 2D vector field of projected cluster angular momenta from microwave maps. Applying this framework to forecast detectability with the Simons Observatory (SO), they show how cross-correlating CMB maps with external galaxy-survey proxies for cluster spin axes can yield high-significance detections, providing a new observational handle on non-thermal rotational pressure support (which biases hydrostatic cluster mass estimates) and cosmic-web tidal spin alignments.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Neural Networks Developed for MBHB Coalescence in the Context of LISA Space Mission
papers.authors: Maria-Catalina Isfan, Laurentiu-Ioan Caramete, Ana Caramete
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly explored to analyse gravitational wave (GW) data expected from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). At the same time, advances in quantum computing have stimulated interest in quantum machine learning as a potential alternative to conventional approaches. We investigate the applicability of quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and classical ML models to two tasks relevant for LISA observations of massive black hole binaries: GW signal detection and merger prediction. Using the Sangria dataset from the LISA Data Challenge, we benchmark several quantum architectures, including variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), post VQC hybrid models, quantum kernel methods, data reuploading classifiers, and quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) networks, against classical support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and LSTM networks. The models are trained on labelled data derived from the Sangria training dataset and evaluated on the corresponding blind dataset. For signal detection, several quantum models match or outperform classical baselines. In particular, the best performing hybrid post VQC architecture correctly identifies all signal samples in the blind dataset, while the standard VQC and data reuploading classifier achieve competitive detection rates. For merger detection and coalescence time estimation, however, the standard VQC emerges as the most reliable model, successfully localising all detected merger events with the lowest localisation errors. We further analyse the trade-offs between predictive performance, model complexity, and quantum circuit resources. Our results indicate that, although no universal quantum advantage is observed, selected quantum models can provide practical benefits for specific GW analysis tasks and represent promising candidates for future LISA data analysis pipelines.

conclusions: For gravitational-wave signal detection in the blind Sangria dataset, a hybrid post-VQC model correctly identifies 100% of signal samples, while the standard VQC and data re-uploading classifier achieve recalls of $\approx 0.996$, outperforming all tested classical baselines.

For merger detection and coalescence time ($t_c$) estimation, the simpler baseline VQC is the most reliable model, successfully localizing 5 out of 6 blind merger events with predicted intervals containing the true $t_c$ and achieving the lowest midpoint timing errors.

More complex architectures do not necessarily generalize better: the top-performing hybrid detection model fails to identify any specific merger events, and both the quantum LSTM and quantum kernel SVM are outperformed by a standard classical SVM.

Because all tests were run on small-scale quantum simulators using engineered classical summary statistics (such as spectral entropy and peak frequency), the results represent a task-specific modeling benefit rather than a formal computational quantum advantage.
ai.summary: The future space-based gravitational-wave observatory LISA will detect coalescing massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) weeks to months before they merge, requiring fast, low-latency analysis pipelines to extract signals buried in complex instrumental noise and astrophysical foregrounds from thousands of Galactic white dwarf binaries. In this paper, the authors explore whether quantum machine learning (QML)—which maps data into quantum states manipulated by parameterized quantum circuits—can outperform classical machine learning at detecting these signals and predicting their merger times ($t_c$). Using simulated one-year time-series strain data from the LISA Data Challenge (the "Sangria" dataset), they extract summary signal-processing features from sliding time windows and benchmark several simulated quantum and hybrid quantum-classical architectures (such as variational quantum classifiers, or VQCs, and quantum LSTMs) against classical baselines (SVMs, MLPs, RNNs, and LSTMs). This provides a systematic test of whether compact quantum circuit models offer practical advantages for realistic gravitational-wave time-series classification and alert generation.

papers.title: Phenomenological implications of cosmic (super)strings with time-varying tension
papers.authors: Anastasios Avgoustidis, Edmund J. Copeland, Adam Moss, Juhan Raidal, Filippo Revello, Gonzalo Villa
papers.abstract: Cosmic strings and cosmic superstrings could have formed in the early universe. In a particular class of models, the tension associated with these defects is time dependent, either because the strings themselves are composed of evolving moduli fields, or because they are directly coupled to evolving scalar fields leading to an effective time dependence in the string tension. Here we take seriously the possibility of this time dependence and investigate the phenomenological consequences of such an evolution, comparing the results to the more traditional case of a fixed time independent tension. In particular, for five different time varying models, motivated by different possible forms of evolution of the string tension, we evaluate their Gravitational Wave (GW) contributions as well as their impact on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). Performing an MCMC analysis of the models we find there are indeed interesting spectral signatures in the GW emission at frequencies between the current PTA and interferometer data, but the signatures are not unique to these strings, making them hard to pin down using current data. However, we do find cosmic strings with evolving tension fit the GW data as well as other favoured models.

conclusions: When the dimensionless string tension remains in the perturbative regime ($G\mu \ll 1$), the backreaction of the string network on the driving scalar field is negligible, meaning the background scalar dynamics and string network evolution can be decoupled.

Tracker and kination solutions for scalar moduli/axions naturally produce power-law ($\mu \propto t^{-m}$) or logarithmic ($\mu \propto \log(t/t_i)$) time evolution in the string tension, which modifies the standard scaling attractors in the VOS network equations.

Time-varying string tensions generate distinct spectral features in the stochastic gravitational wave background at intermediate frequencies between Pulsar Timing Array ($\sim 10^{-8}\text{ Hz}$) and ground/space interferometer bands.

MCMC fits to NANOGrav 15-year, LVK O3, and CMB data show that evolving-tension cosmic strings fit current gravitational wave observations as well as standard constant-tension superstring models, though their spectral signatures are degenerate with other cosmological scenarios in current data.
ai.summary: Cosmic strings—one-dimensional topological defects formed during early-universe symmetry-breaking phase transitions or as fundamental strings stretched to macroeconomic scales in string theory—form networks that emit a stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background across many decades of frequency as oscillating string loops decay. While standard analyses assume a constant string tension $\mu$ (mass per unit length), string compactifications naturally couple this tension to dynamically evolving scalar fields (such as moduli or axions rolling down exponential potentials), causing $G\mu(t)$ to vary over cosmic time. The authors first show analytically that the string network's backreaction on the scalar field is negligible for perturbative tensions ($G\mu \ll 1$), and then extend the velocity-dependent one-scale (VOS) network evolution equations to model five phenomenological tension-evolution profiles (including continuous power-law, truncated, window, top-hat, and axion-kination evolutions). By running MCMC fits against NANOGrav 15-year Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) data, LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) O3 bounds, and CMB anisotropy constraints, they explore whether evolving string tensions can explain the nanohertz GW background and leave testable signatures for future multi-band GW observatories.

papers.title: Extracting non-Gaussian information of line-intensity maps with weighted skew spectra
papers.authors: Eleonora Vanzan, Azadeh Moradinezhad Dizgah, Ely D. Kovetz
papers.abstract: The bispectrum of line-intensity maps carries cosmological and astrophysical information beyond the power spectrum, but its large data vector hampers the analysis of survey data. Skew spectra address this by compressing the bispectrum into a handful of power-spectrum-like observables, cross-spectra of the observed field with filtered squares of it. We present the first application of optimally weighted skew spectra to line-intensity mapping of galaxy-hosted emission, where all clustering and shot-noise terms are luminosity weighted and the mean intensity is unknown. We perform idealized real-space Fisher forecasts for a SPHEREx-like survey of H$\alpha$ emission at $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4.6$, in its deep fields and in a noisier all-sky configuration. First, the compression carries over to intensity maps: on perturbative scales and for a fixed redshift evolution of the emitters, four skew spectra, one of them matched to the shot noise, recover the bispectrum constraints on biases, shot noise and cosmological parameters to within a few percent. Second, the joint analysis of the power spectrum and the skew spectra measures the ratios of the second-order biases to the linear bias in each redshift bin. Within a bin the biases are degenerate with the unknown mean intensity, but their ratios are not, so their redshift evolution is measured without a model for the emitters. For emission that depends on halo mass alone, these ratios are determined by luminosity-weighted averages of the halo biases, so their evolution can test the halo-emission connection, including dependence on assembly history or environment. The bias ratios are not accessible to the tree-level real-space power spectrum alone. At $z \lesssim 3$ an all-sky SPHEREx-like configuration can detect departures of order $0.1$ in the bias ratios at $3\sigma$, while deeper fields perform better in the highest-redshift bins.

conclusions: Four weighted skew spectra—three standard clustering kernels plus a fourth kernel matched to the shot noise—recover the full tree-level bispectrum constraints on bias parameters within $3\%$, shot-noise parameters within $1\%$, and cosmological parameters within $2\%$.

Approximating the pair-weighted shot-noise bias $b_1^{[L^2]}$ as equal to the standard luminosity-weighted bias $b_1$ misweights the mixed shot-clustering bispectrum term by up to $20\%$ across the survey redshift range ($0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4.6$).

In a model-independent per-bin joint analysis with the power spectrum, the ratios $b_2/b_1$ and $b_{\mathcal{G}_2}/b_1$ are measured independently of the unknown mean intensity $\langle I \rangle$; an all-sky SPHEREx-like survey constrains $b_2/b_1$ to $10\%$ at $z \le 1.2$ and detects $\sim 0.1$ departures in the bias ratios at $3\sigma$ for $z \lesssim 3$, directly testing whether line emission depends on halo assembly history or environment.

When cosmological parameters are varied in the per-bin joint analysis, the different scaling with the matter power spectrum breaks the degeneracy between $\langle I \rangle b_1$ and $\sigma_8(z)$, yielding a real-space measurement of $\sigma_8(z)$ to $\sim 10\%$ around $z \sim 1.5$ in the all-sky configuration without assuming an emission model.

While the three-point correlation function in Fourier space (the bispectrum) can break this degeneracy and probe higher-order galaxy biases, its massive data vector makes full survey covariance estimation and analysis computationally prohibitive. In this paper, the authors extend "weighted skew spectra"—fast, two-point cross-correlations between the observed intensity field and filtered quadratic products of itself—to galaxy-hosted LIM, introducing a dedicated fourth filter kernel to capture luminosity-weighted shot noise alongside the three standard tree-level perturbation theory clustering kernels. Using idealized real-space Fisher forecasts for a SPHEREx-like $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ survey across $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4.6$, they show that just four skew spectra compress nearly all the cosmological and astrophysical information of the full bispectrum and allow a joint analysis with the power spectrum to measure non-linear bias ratios ($b_2/b_1$ and tidal bias $b_{\mathcal{G}_2}/b_1$) completely independently of the unknown mean intensity.

papers.title: At the EDGES of MADness: phenomenology of relic millicharged atomic dark matter
papers.authors: Eleonora Vanzan, Kimberly K. Boddy, Ely D. Kovetz
papers.abstract: Millicharged dark matter lives in a corner of parameter space that has been considerably shrinking over the past decades, due to constraints from cosmology, astrophysical systems, and ground-based experiments. A particularly interesting probe is the 21-cm absorption signal at Cosmic Dawn, which attracted interest in light of the EDGES claim: the reported excess absorption can be explained by millicharged dark matter with a fractional electric charge of~$10^{-6} \lesssim \epsilon \lesssim 10^{-4}$, but it must be a subpercent of the total dark matter abundance to remain consistent with the cosmic microwave background (CMB). We show that very low fractions of millicharged dark matter naturally arise from atomic dark matter: a dark sector model that replicates the physics of standard atomic hydrogen. Dark ions undergo the process of dark recombination, leaving a relic ionized component that, in the presence of kinetic mixing, is naturally millicharged. We modify the cosmological Boltzmann solver CLASS to incorporate this scenario, and we investigate the parameter space of millicharged atomic dark matter (MAD) that is allowed by CMB, large-scale structure, and supernovae data. We find there are cosmologically viable regions of MAD parameter space that are consistent with laboratory and astrophysical bounds and also overlap with the EDGES-defined window. Although the EDGES result is likely not a Cosmic Dawn signal, MAD leaves distinctive cosmological signatures, accessible to upcoming 21-cm observations.

conclusions: Current CMB, BAO, large-scale structure, and supernova data place a strict upper limit on the extra relativistic degrees of freedom from the dark radiation bath of $\Delta N_D \lesssim 0.3$, while leaving the microphysical dark-sector parameters largely unconstrained when dark recombination occurs early enough.

Viable regions of the parameter space span fractional electric charges of $10^{-6} \lesssim \epsilon \lesssim 10^{-4}$ and $\epsilon \lesssim 10^{-8}$ with dark fermion masses $\gtrsim 10\,\text{MeV}$ (including a broad compatibility band around $m_{e_D} \sim 10\,\text{MeV}$), where the dark proton mass naturally sets the sub-percent relic ionized fraction required to cool baryons at Cosmic Dawn in line with the EDGES window.

In the $H_0$–$S_8$ plane, the model behaves similarly to pure atomic dark matter—any alleviation of the Hubble and $S_8$ tensions is driven primarily by the dark radiation component and dark acoustic oscillations rather than the millicharge interaction itself.

Scenarios with late dark recombination can remain nearly indistinguishable from $\Lambda\text{CDM}$ or pure atomic dark matter in primary CMB and linear matter power spectrum observables, yet still strongly alter the late-time thermal history of baryons, offering a clear target for upcoming 21-cm line-intensity mapping surveys.

However, to avoid distorting the cosmic microwave background (CMB), this interacting component can only make up a sub-percent ($\lesssim 0.4\%$) fraction of the total dark matter, a tiny fraction that usually has to be put in by hand. The authors show that this sub-percent fraction arises naturally in "atomic dark matter" (ADM) models—where dark protons and dark electrons bind into neutral dark hydrogen via a dark photon—if kinetic mixing between the dark and visible photons gives the small leftover ionized fraction from dark recombination an effective millicharge. They implement this Millicharged Atomic Dark Matter (MAD) model into the Boltzmann solver `CLASS`, self-consistently tracking dark recombination, dark acoustic oscillations, and dark-visible heat and momentum exchange to constrain the parameter space against CMB, BAO, supernova, and large-scale structure data.

papers.title: Theoretical Consistency and Observational Constraints on Entropic Cosmology
papers.authors: Yunliang Ren, Xiaofeng Yang, Xuwei Zhang, Shuangnan Chen, Yangjun Shi, Hoernisa Iminniyaza
papers.abstract: Recent DESI DR2 results suggest that dark energy may evolve with time, which motivates a re-examination of entropic cosmology. In this work, we study three representative entropic models, denoted as Models A, B, and C, corresponding to the driving terms $H^2$, $H^2+\dot H$, and $H^2+\dot H+H^4$, respectively. We establish a general framework for entropic cosmology and examine these models through early universe consistency, the Trans-Planckian Censorship Conjecture (TCC), and the realization of Quintom-B crossing. We constrain these models using the Pantheon+ sample, DESI DR2 BAO measurements, and Planck 2018 CMB distance priors, and compare their fits to the data. For Model C, we adopt a first-order perturbative treatment in the full data analysis to maintain numerical stability in the presence of the higher-order term. We find that Model A is the simplest among the three models, but it is difficult to make it compatible with both early universe consistency and the TCC condition. Model B, which includes a derivative correction term, shows a small difference in the fit to observational data compared to Model A, and is more consistent with the theoretical constraints. Model C includes more correction terms, but does not provide a better fit to the data. The parameter region favored by observations does not fully overlap with that preferred by theoretical consistency, which suggests that entropic cosmology may require further development to achieve a self-consistent description across different cosmic epochs.

conclusions: The simplest entropic model (Model A, driving term $\propto H^2$) is statistically preferred by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) due to having fewer parameters, but fails to simultaneously satisfy early-universe matter/radiation domination and the Trans-Planckian Censorship Conjecture (TCC).

Adding a time-derivative term (Model B, $\propto H^2 + \dot{H}$) suppresses high-redshift entropic effects and allows a future transition out of accelerated expansion, making it the best compromise between observational fit and theoretical consistency.

Including a higher-order quantum-motivated correction (Model C, adding $\propto H^4$) requires a first-order perturbative expansion to remain numerically stable at high redshift, and CMB distance priors drive its coefficient $\tilde{\beta}_3$ very close to zero.

Across all three formulations, the parameter regions favored by background observations (Pantheon+, DESI DR2, Planck 2018) do not fully overlap with those required for theoretical consistency across cosmic epochs, showing that standard entropic parameterizations struggle to act as a complete replacement for dark energy.

ai.summary: Entropic cosmology attempts to explain late-time cosmic acceleration without a cosmological constant by treating the cosmic horizon as a thermodynamic boundary with Bekenstein-Hawking entropy and temperature, which generates an outward "entropic force" modifying the Friedmann equations. Motivated by recent DESI DR2 hints of evolving dark energy, the authors test three effective entropic driving terms—proportional to $H^2$ (Model A), $H^2 + \dot{H}$ (Model B), and $H^2 + \dot{H} + H^4$ (Model C)—against three theoretical criteria: standard early-universe expansion, the Trans-Planckian Censorship Conjecture (TCC, a quantum-gravity condition requiring sub-Planckian fluctuations to never cross the Hubble horizon, which restricts eternal acceleration), and "Quintom-B" crossing (where the effective dark energy equation of state $w_{\rm DE}$ crosses $-1$ from below to above). They then confront the background expansion histories of these models with Pantheon+ Type Ia supernovae, DESI DR2 BAO, and Planck 2018 CMB distance priors. This study is important because it shows that while horizon thermodynamics can mimic dynamical dark energy, the parameter space favored by late- and early-time distance measurements is in tension with the theoretical requirements for a self-consistent cosmic history.

papers.title: Going off the (momentum) grid: A simple implementation of noncold relics in linear Boltzmann solvers
papers.authors: Arad Nasiri, Murali Saravanan, Caio B. de S. Nascimento
papers.abstract: Linear Boltzmann solvers typically evolve the perturbations of noncold relics, such as massive neutrinos or hot subcomponents of the dark matter, on a momentum grid, often switching to a fluid approximation on small scales for efficiency. We implement in CLASS the Dispersive Fluid Approximation (DFA), a fluid scheme that captures the scale-dependent sound speed of these species. Within the standard ncdm module, the DFA significantly outperforms the default CLASS fluid approximation in the cross and neutrino power spectra, and reduces errors in the cold dark matter power spectrum by up to an order of magnitude, while adding only 1-4% to the total runtime. We also present the first open-source implementation of the Generalized Boltzmann Hierarchy (GBH), which simplifies the implementation of noncold relics by integrating out the momentum dependence of their perturbations altogether. Combined with the DFA and tested on massive neutrinos, the GBH reproduces the matter power spectrum to better than permille accuracy and cosmological parameter constraints to better than 0.05 sigma, at a computational cost comparable to that of the standard implementation. We argue that the GBH is particularly well suited to non-thermal relics whose distribution function varies with time or across parameter space. Our implementation of both the DFA and the GBH in CLASS is publicly available at this https URL .

conclusions: Replacing the default CLASS fluid approximation with the Dispersive Fluid Approximation (DFA) inside the standard `ncdm` module cuts cold dark matter power spectrum errors by up to an order of magnitude and keeps low-redshift neutrino auto-power spectrum errors below $\sim 10\%$ across all scales (compared to a factor of $\sim 2$ error in default CLASS), while adding only $1\text{--}4\%$ to total runtime.

Combining the momentum-integrated Generalized Boltzmann Hierarchy (GBH) with the DFA reproduces reference neutrino transfer functions and the total matter power spectrum to better than permille ($< 10^{-3}$) accuracy at a total runtime overhead of $6\text{--}8\%$ over default CLASS ($\sim 1.2\times$ the time spent in the massive neutrino sector).

Full MCMC parameter inference on Planck PR3 CMB temperature, polarization, and lensing data for $\Lambda\text{CDM} + M_\nu$ shows that GBH + DFA recovers cosmological parameter posteriors and $M_\nu$ upper limits to within $0.05\sigma$ of the standard momentum-grid implementation.

Pushing the GBH-to-DFA transition too deep into the sub-horizon regime causes numerical instabilities from accumulated truncation errors at high velocity-weight order $n_{\max}$, establishing an empirical stability ceiling of $\texttt{gbh\_FA\_trigger} \lesssim 25(M_\nu/\text{eV})^{-0.21}$ (with a safe default of $15$).

ai.summary: In linear Boltzmann solvers like CLASS and CAMB, evolving "noncold relics"—particles with significant thermal velocities like massive neutrinos or warm/freeze-in dark matter that free-stream and suppress small-scale structure—is computationally expensive because their perturbations depend on both scale and particle momentum. Standard codes discretize this momentum on a grid tailored to a thermal Fermi-Dirac distribution and switch to a crude fluid approximation deep inside the free-streaming scale, an approach that loses efficiency when applied to exotic relics with non-thermal or time-varying momentum distributions. In this paper, the authors implement two new techniques into CLASS: the Generalized Boltzmann Hierarchy (GBH), which integrates out momentum entirely in favor of a hierarchy of velocity-weighted fluid moments, and the Dispersive Fluid Approximation (DFA), an improved small-scale closure that captures the scale-dependent sound speed of the dispersive relic fluid. This matters because it simplifies the linear perturbation equations by removing the momentum grid, improves the accuracy of small-scale neutrino and matter power spectra at negligible computational cost, and makes it much easier to run parameter scans for non-thermal dark matter models without manually re-tuning momentum quadrature grids.

papers.title: Toward a Complete Interpretation of Global 21 cm Absorption Signals Using the Radio CMB
papers.authors: Hannah Fronenberg
papers.abstract: The global 21 cm signal is among the most direct probes of cosmic dawn, encoding information about when the first stars formed and how efficiently they heated their surroundings. However, such measurements are limited by bright Galactic foregrounds, ionospheric effects, and instrumental systematics. Even a confident detection would face a further obstacle: the brightness temperature depends on the spin temperature of the gas and the temperature of the radio background only through a single combination, so anomalous signals such as the EDGES (Bowman et al. 2018) absorption trough admit both cold gas and excess radio background interpretations. Recently, Holder et al. 2026 showed that resonant 21 cm absorption by high-redshift neutral hydrogen imprints an excess optical depth on CMB anisotropies at radio wavelengths, which depends on the spin temperature alone. Here we propose combining a measurement of the CMB hydrogen optical depth with the global signal to break this degeneracy, isolating the radio background temperature without the need for astrophysical modelling. Forecasting four interferometric configurations, we find that a compact $55 \times 55$ array of 6 m dishes observing for 4000 hours can establish an EDGES-like optical depth at $4.2\sigma$, while fiducial cosmic dawn histories require roughly an order of magnitude more collecting area. This constitutes a model-independent route to interpreting any global 21 cm detection.

conclusions: Resonant 21 cm absorption during cosmic dawn suppresses radio CMB anisotropies by a factor $\alpha = e^{-\tau_{\rm HI}}$, where $\tau_{\rm HI} \propto x_{\rm HI}/T_s$ depends only on the spin temperature and is completely insensitive to any excess radio background ($T_R$).

An anomalously cold EDGES-like thermal history implies $\tau_{\rm HI} \approx 0.197$ (an extra $14\%$–$17.5\%$ suppression of CMB fluctuations relative to standard cosmic dawn models, which have $\tau_{\rm HI} \approx 0.04$).

A compact "Robust" interferometer of $55 \times 55$ (3,025) 6 m dishes observing $f_{\rm sky}=0.1$ for 4,000 hours can establish an EDGES-like excess optical depth at $4.23\sigma$ ($\sigma_{\rm null}$), whereas standard fiducial histories only reach $1.19\sigma$ (at $z=17.2$) to $1.77\sigma$ (at $z=12.25$) and would require $\sim 10^4$ dishes for a $3\sigma$ constraint.

Smaller dishes (6 m vs. HERA's 14 m) are essential because the shortest baseline sets the minimum multipole ($\ell_{\min} \gtrsim 10$), and sensitivity is driven by the largest angular scales where the CMB power spectrum $C_\ell$ is brightest.
ai.summary: During cosmic dawn ($z \sim 12\text{--}20$), radiation from the first stars couples the 21 cm hyperfine "spin temperature" ($T_s$) of neutral hydrogen to the cold intergalactic gas, creating a sky-averaged ("global") 21 cm absorption trough against the background radio radiation ($T_R$). However, the global brightness temperature $T_b \propto (1 - T_R/T_s)$ suffers from a fundamental degeneracy: an anomalously deep absorption signal—like the famous 2018 EDGES claim—could be caused either by exotic physics cooling the gas ($T_s \ll T_{\rm adiabatic}$) or by an excess radio background above the CMB ($T_R > T_{\rm CMB}$). Building on recent work showing that resonant 21 cm absorption at cosmic dawn also acts like an extra screen that dims CMB temperature anisotropies at radio frequencies ($\sim 60\text{--}120\text{ MHz}$) by $e^{-\tau_{\rm HI}}$ where the optical depth $\tau_{\rm HI} \propto x_{\rm HI}/T_s$, the author proposes cross-correlating low-frequency radio interferometer maps with high-precision Planck millimeter CMB templates. By measuring this template suppression amplitude alongside the global 21 cm signal, one can directly measure $T_s$ and break the $T_s$–$T_R$ degeneracy without relying on astrophysical models.

papers.title: Cosmological lensing as a jump process
papers.authors: Galymzhan Baltabay, Ville Vaskonen
papers.abstract: We develop a jump-process formalism for the probability density function (PDF) of gravitational lensing fields. In the Born approximation, each lens adds a jump to the convergence $\kappa$ and the two components of the shear, making lensing a jump process in redshift. For independent lenses, the joint PDF of the lensing fields obeys a compensated Kolmogorov-Feller equation, which we solve in closed form in Fourier space and extend to clustered lenses using their two-point correlation function. A Fourier-Hankel inversion then yields the joint PDF of $\kappa$ and the shear magnitude $\gamma$, from which the magnification PDF follows, including its high-magnification tail, without sampling noise. We use these PDFs to train an updated version of the FLUMEN emulator, which makes likelihood-based inference from the full magnification distribution feasible across cosmologies. To motivate such analyses, we estimate that samples of $10^4$ Roman supernovae, $10^5$ Rubin supernovae, 300 Einstein Telescope standard sirens, and 12 LISA standard sirens could constrain the matter fluctuation amplitude $\sigma_8$ respectively to 4.8\%, 5.1\%, 8.5\%, and 19\%, with the other cosmological parameters fixed.

conclusions: Treating lensing in the Born approximation as a jump process governed by a compensated Kolmogorov–Feller equation yields noise-free joint PDFs of $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ across all image parities (types I, II, and III), seamlessly capturing the $\mu^{-2}$ fold-caustic scaling in the high-magnification tail without Monte Carlo sampling.

The updated FLUMEN neural network emulator, trained on 4372 noise-free PDFs across a 10-dimensional parameter space (including $\Omega_K$, $w_0$, $w_a$, and $z_s \in [0.2, 12]$) with a derivative-penalized loss function, reproduces the analytical magnification PDFs to a median maximum deviation of $0.29\%$ of the peak.

The high-magnification tail responds much more strongly to the matter clustering amplitude $\sigma_8$ than the bulk width of the distribution: at $z_s = 1$, a $10\%$ increase in $\sigma_8$ changes the width $\sigma_{\ln\mu}$ by $\sim 9\%$ but boosts the probability of high magnification $P(\mu > 1.5)$ by $35\%$.

Idealized Fisher forecasts (fixing other cosmological parameters) show that lensing scatter alone could constrain $\sigma_8$ to $4.8\%$ with $10^4$ Roman SNe, $5.1\%$ with $10^5$ Rubin SNe, $8.5\%$ with 300 Einstein Telescope standard sirens, and $19\%$ with 12 LISA standard sirens.

ai.summary: When light or gravitational waves from distant standard candles and sirens travel through the cosmic web, intervening halos and filaments magnify or demagnify their signals, creating a skewed probability distribution of magnifications ($\mu$) whose shape and high-magnification tail encode the amplitude of matter clustering ($\sigma_8$). Traditionally, predicting this magnification probability density function (PDF) requires expensive ray-tracing through $N$-body simulations or Monte Carlo sampling, both of which suffer from severe shot noise in the rare, high-magnification tail. In this paper, the authors formulate gravitational lensing under the Born approximation as a stochastic jump process in redshift, where each encountered halo (with subhalos) and filament adds a discrete jump to the convergence $\kappa$ and shear $(\gamma_1, \gamma_2)$. By solving the resulting master equation (a compensated Kolmogorov–Feller equation) analytically in Fourier space—including a linear-bias two-halo clustering term—and inverting it via a Fourier–Hankel transform, they obtain exact, sampling-noise-free joint PDFs of $\kappa$, $\gamma$, and $\mu$. They then use these noise-free predictions to train an upgraded version of the FLUMEN neural network emulator across a 10-parameter $w_0 w_a$CDM + $\Omega_K$ space, enabling fast likelihood inference and Fisher forecasts for upcoming supernova and gravitational-wave surveys.

papers.title: Cosmological tests of chameleon dark energy with dark sector coupling
papers.authors: Jia-Qi Wang, Zong-Kuan Guo, Shao-Jiang Wang
papers.abstract: Recent DESI measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations favor a value of $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$ different from that preferred by Planck cosmic microwave background observations. Combined with supernova data, these observations suggest an evolving dark energy equation of state that crosses $w=-1$. As a potential solution to multiple cosmological problems, chameleon dark energy has attracted increasing attention in recent years. In this work, we constrain a chameleon model in which late-time cosmic acceleration is driven by a canonical scalar field nonminimally coupled to dark matter. At early times, the scalar field evolves under the combined influence of its potential and the nonminimal coupling, and its effective mass greatly exceeds the Hubble parameter. The chameleon model with energy transfer from dark energy to dark matter yields a best-fit improvement of $\Delta\chi^2=-7.25$ relative to $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$, comparable to that for energy transfer in the opposite direction. Joint sampling over both coupling directions favors a nonzero interaction at $3.3\sigma$. Although no phantom field is introduced, the modified dark matter evolution produces an effective dark energy equation of state that crosses $w=-1$ at $z\simeq0.5$.

conclusions: Joint sampling over both coupling signs favors a nonzero dark-sector interaction at $3.3\sigma$ ($\beta = 0.186^{+0.047}_{-0.038}$ and $n < 0.0703$ for the chameleon branch $\beta>0$), improving the fit over $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ by $\Delta\chi^2_{\min} = -7.25$ and receiving $49.1\%$ of the posterior weight against $50.9\%$ for the runaway $\beta<0$ branch.

Because energy transfers from dark energy to dark matter at late times in the chameleon branch, dark matter dilutes more slowly than $a^{-3}$, generating an effective equation of state $w_{\mathrm{DE}}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ that crosses $w=-1$ from below to above at $z_{\mathrm{cross}} \simeq 0.487$ while the physical scalar field remains canonical ($w_\varphi \geq -1$).

The early-time chameleon tracking phase leaves the sound horizon and inferred Hubble constant nearly unchanged from $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ ($H_0 = 67.57^{+0.50}_{-0.41}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$), whereas the late-time fifth force and altered dark matter dilution boost structure growth to $S_8 = 0.873 \pm 0.025$ (compared to $0.8142 \pm 0.0072$ in $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$).

Replacing DES-Dovekie with Pantheon+ or Union3.1 supernova data yields virtually identical parameter constraints and comparable Bayesian support for the chameleon branch ($P(\beta>0) \simeq 39.5\%$ and $44.0\%$, respectively), demonstrating robustness across SN calibrations.

The authors investigate the "chameleon" branch of this model—where an inverse-power-law potential $V(\varphi) \propto \varphi^{-n}$ balances an exponential coupling $\mathcal{A}(\varphi)=e^{\beta\varphi}$ ($\beta>0$) that transfers energy from dark energy to dark matter, creating an environment-dependent effective mass $m_{\mathrm{eff}}$—by implementing an implicit stiff ODE solver in `CAMB` to evolve the background and linear perturbations and running `PolyChord` nested sampling against Planck PR4 + ACT DR6 CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and DES-Dovekie (plus Pantheon+ and Union3.1) supernovae. papers.title: UNIONS: Red and blue alignments of DESI DR1 galaxies
papers.authors: R. Paviot, C. Murray, M. Kilbinger, C. Daley, F. Hervas-Peters, A. Corinaldi, T. de Boer, S. Guerrini, M. J. Hudson, G. S. H. Paek, L. Van Waerbeke, J. Yun
papers.abstract: Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are a dominant source of systematics in weak-lensing cosmological analyses, and direct measurements on spectroscopic samples are the primary source of priors on their amplitude. We measure the IA of galaxies from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) as a function of colour, stellar mass, and halo mass, by cross-correlating the DESI spectroscopic catalogues with the weak-lensing shape catalogue of the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS) over up to 2400 deg$^2$. We fit the three-dimensional galaxy-galaxy and galaxy-shape multipoles of the DESI BGS, LRG, and ELG samples, split by colour and stellar mass, with the non-linear linear alignment (NLA) and the tidal alignment and tidal torquing (TATT) models. Halo masses are measured for the BGS red sample from galaxy-galaxy lensing and extended to the LRGs through the resulting stellar-to-halo mass relation. Red galaxies are strongly and radially aligned, but their alignment amplitude is not a single power law of halo mass between $6\times10^{11}$ and $3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$: it is nearly flat at low mass and rises steeply above a break at $1.3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$. Massive blue BGS galaxies instead show a tangential alignment, detected at $3.3\sigma$, to our knowledge the most significant detection of a non-zero alignment of blue galaxies to date, while the low-mass blue BGS galaxies and the ELGs are consistent with zero. At our current precision, the data do not favour TATT over NLA.

conclusions: Red galaxies exhibit strong radial alignment, but their alignment amplitude $A_{\rm IA}$ does not follow a single power law with halo mass between $6\times 10^{11}$ and $3\times 10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$; instead, it follows a broken power law that stays nearly flat ($A_{\rm IA} \approx 1\text{--}2$) at low masses and rises steeply above a break at $M_b = 1.3\times 10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$.

Massive blue galaxies in the BGS sample show a statistically significant tangential alignment (stretching perpendicular to matter overdensities) detected at $3.3\sigma$, whereas low-mass blue galaxies and high-redshift ELGs ($0.8 < z < 1.6$) are consistent with zero alignment ($-1.4 < A_{\rm IA} < 0.7$ at $2\sigma$).

At current precision, Bayesian model comparison does not favour the higher-order TATT model over the simpler NLA model for blue galaxies, as the tangential alignment signal is captured by a negative linear tidal-alignment amplitude rather than the quadratic tidal-torquing term.
Using 3D redshift-space multipoles instead of traditional projected correlation functions ($w_{g+}$) reduces the uncertainties on the alignment amplitudes by $20\text{--}43\%$ on identical data.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides observational background on intrinsic alignments—a key weak-lensing systematic for Euclid—and uses DESI DR1 clustering multipoles, though it does not directly involve beyond-ΛCDM simulations, emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In weak gravitational lensing surveys, measuring the subtle coherent distortions of background galaxy images (cosmic shear) is complicated by intrinsic alignments (IA)—the tendency of physically nearby galaxies to align their shapes with the surrounding large-scale tidal field, mimicking the lensing signal. Because most direct IA measurements have focused on bright, massive red galaxies, we lack tight empirical priors on the fainter and bluer galaxy populations that actually dominate cosmic-shear catalogues. The authors cross-correlate spectroscopic galaxy positions from DESI DR1 (spanning Bright Galaxy Survey, Luminous Red Galaxy, and Emission Line Galaxy samples) with galaxy shape measurements from the northern UNIONS imaging survey over up to $2400\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. By fitting three-dimensional redshift-space clustering monopoles and galaxy-shape quadrupoles with the Non-Linear Alignment (NLA) and Tidal Alignment and Tidal Torquing (TATT) models—and calibrating halo masses via galaxy-galaxy lensing—they map out IA across colour, stellar mass, and halo mass. These measurements show that extrapolating simple single-power-law IA priors from bright galaxies to faint weak-lensing sources is inaccurate, directly informing how Stage-IV surveys like Euclid must model IA systematics.

papers.title: OCCAMS: A Multi-Task Learning-Based Investigation of the CMB Power Spectra
papers.authors: Ankit Mandal, Rahul Shah, Md. Wali Hossain, Somasri Sen, Anjan A Sen, Supratik Pal
papers.abstract: How many latent variables are needed to fit the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarisation power spectra when a neural network is given no cosmological model, and to what extent do they map onto the standard cosmological parameters? We use multi-task learning with variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated spectra (TT, TE, EE) over $2\le\ell\le2500$. No cosmological model is built into the network, and the number of latent variables, $L$, is varied over $L=5$, $6$ and $7$. Their fits are compared to the Planck 2018 data using $\hat{\chi}^2$, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Their correspondence with cosmological parameters is measured with normalised mutual information post-training. The loss weights are set within a single training run by uncertainty weighting, with the weight of the disentanglement term either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). The reconstruction loss is split over multipole ranges in three configurations that separate the roles of temperature and polarisation and of the low- and high-$\ell$ ranges. In four of the six combinations of configuration and strategy, the fit improves from $L=5$ to $L=6$ and not beyond, and $L=6$ is the best, or close to the best, in five of the six cases. So, six latent variables are needed, as many as the free parameters of the standard, model-dependent approach. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of the disentanglement weight and has the higher evidence at $L=5$ and $6$: the two strategies are points on a trade-off between interpretability and fit to the data. Notably, the latent variables for $\tau$ and $A_s$ share almost no information in any model, consistent with large-scale polarisation separating the two, as in standard analyses. A deep-learning approach can thus give a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.

conclusions: When extending the CMB angular power spectra down to $\ell = 2$ and including polarization ($TT, TE, EE$), $L = 6$ latent variables are optimal or within $\ln B \simeq 1$ of the best model in 5 of the 6 loss configurations—recovering the 6 degrees of freedom of standard $\Lambda$CDM, whereas previous $\ell \ge 30$ studies only needed 5 because $A_s$ and $\tau$ are degenerate via $A_s e^{-2\tau}$ at small scales.

The latent variables representing $\tau$ and $A_s$ share virtually no mutual information (normalised MI $\le 0.03$) across all 18 trained models, confirming that the network independently discovers how the large-scale $EE$ reionization bump breaks the $A_s$–$\tau$ degeneracy.

Parameters with sharp, localized spectral signatures ($\omega_b$, followed by $\tau$, $\omega_{\mathrm{cdm}}$, and $h$) map cleanly onto individual latent variables, whereas $A_s$ and $n_s$ are captured least cleanly with small cross-terms indicating partially overlapping smooth effects.

Comparing hyperparameter tuning strategies reveals a trade-off between physical interpretability and statistical fit: fixing a high disentanglement penalty (semi-automated, SA) yields cleaner parameter separation (mean score $0.58$ vs. $0.40$), while learning all weights automatically (completely automated, CA) achieves higher Bayesian evidence on Planck 2018 data (with reduced $\hat{\chi}^2$ between $0.955$ and $0.988$ across all models).
ai.relevance_reason: While the paper focuses on CMB power spectra rather than late-time LSS or beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations, its use of variational autoencoders and multi-task uncertainty weighting to build compact ML surrogates of power spectra is loosely relevant background for emulator design.
ai.summary: When fitting the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), we normally assume the six parameters of $\Lambda$CDM in advance, even though the data often constrain combinations of parameters rather than individual ones. This paper asks how many independent degrees of freedom the CMB temperature and polarization power spectra ($TT$, $TE$, $EE$) actually require when compressed by a deep neural network with no built-in cosmological model. The authors use a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)—a neural network that compresses input data into a low-dimensional "latent space" bottleneck before reconstructing it—trained on 200,000 CLASS-generated spectra across the full multipole range $2 \le \ell \le 2500$, using multi-task uncertainty weighting to automatically balance reconstruction accuracy against latent-variable disentanglement in a single training run. Testing latent dimensions $L=5, 6, 7$ against Planck 2018 data, they demonstrate that including large-scale polarization ($\ell < 30$) forces the network to require six latent variables rather than five, naturally recovering the dimensionality and physical parameter separation of $\Lambda$CDM directly from the spectra.

papers.title: An Empirically Calibrated [C II] Luminosity-Halo Mass Relation for Line Intensity Mapping
papers.authors: Oliver Jeong, Martin White
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave line intensity mapping aims to observe the high-redshift universe through the 158 $\mu$m fine-structure line of [C II], the brightest far-infrared line of star-forming galaxies. Whether a [C II] experiment at $z>4$ measures the clustering of large-scale structure, which carries rich cosmological information, rather than the shot noise of the emitters depends on the amplitude and the shape of the [C II] power spectrum. Forecasts often build the power spectrum from a halo mass--luminosity relation, $L(M_h)$, chained from scaling relations measured in other regimes or read off simulations, without a quantified uncertainty. We instead calibrate a double power-law $L(M_h,z)$ on [C II] data alone: the mean [C II] intensity from tomographic cross-correlation at $0.4<z<4.2$ and the luminosity-function measurements and limits at $z\simeq0$ and $4.3\lesssim z\lesssim8$. The four parameters of the double power law are fitted at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$ separately, with no assumption about their evolution, and then jointly across $0<z<7$, and we examine how the uncertainty depends on the modeling assumptions. The shape of the power spectrum is settled by the existing data. The clustering peak stands a factor of $45\,(23$-$93)$ and $64\,(38$-$112)$ above the shot-noise floor at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$, and the two cross at $k_c\simeq0.37$ and $0.44\,h$Mpc$^{-1}$. The amplitude is known less well, the clustering power to $0.5-0.6$ dex and the shot noise to $0.7-0.9$ dex. The results show that the signal comes from halos accessible by current galaxy surveys, those that host the Lyman-break galaxies and Ly$\alpha$ emitters at these redshifts. The luminosity-weighted bias is relatively high, with values of $4-5$.

conclusions: The large-scale clustering peak of the [C II] power spectrum stands a factor of $45\,(23\text{--}93)$ at $z=4.5$ and $64\,(38\text{--}112)$ at $z=5.5$ above the shot-noise floor, crossing the shot noise at $k_c \simeq 0.37$ and $0.44\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ respectively, meaning cosmological clustering is cleanly separable from discrete emitter noise on large scales ($k < k_c$).

While the shape of the power spectrum is tightly constrained by existing [C II] data, its overall amplitude remains uncertain—with the clustering power known to $0.5\text{--}0.6\,\text{dex}$ and the shot noise to $0.7\text{--}0.9\,\text{dex}$.

About $90\%$ of the mean [C II] intensity originates from halos within a decade around the break mass ($M_h \sim 10^{11}\text{--}10^{12}\,M_\odot$, with $\log_{10}(M_1/M_\odot) = 11.66^{+0.39}_{-0.33}$ at $z=4.5$ and $11.26^{+0.30}_{-0.25}$ at $z=5.5$), which are the same halos that already host UV-selected Lyman-break galaxies and $\text{Ly}\alpha$ emitters.

The inferred luminosity-weighted tracer bias is high ($b_{\text{eff}} \simeq 3.9\text{--}4.3$), making [C II] LIM a sensitive probe of scale-dependent bias from local primordial non-Gaussianity ($f_{\text{NL}}$) if large-scale foregrounds are controlled.

Extending luminosity function measurements to fainter or brighter galaxies barely shrinks the power spectrum amplitude uncertainty; instead, measuring the mean [C II] luminosity in halo-mass bins to $0.2\,\text{dex}$ via galaxy stacking or galaxy–LIM cross-correlations would halve the shot-noise and brightness-temperature uncertainties.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful background on halo-model tracer bias and power spectrum modelling for high-redshift line intensity mapping, though it focuses on empirical astrophysical scaling relations in standard $\Lambda$CDM rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Line intensity mapping (LIM) measures the aggregate spatial fluctuations of a spectral emission line across all galaxies in a volume without resolving individual sources, using the $158\,\mu\text{m}$ fine-structure cooling line of singly ionized carbon ([C II]) as a prime tracer of the high-redshift ($z > 4$) universe. A key question for upcoming millimeter-wave LIM surveys is whether the large-scale clustering signal—which encodes cosmological information—stands clearly above the flat Poisson shot-noise floor caused by discrete galaxy emitters. Rather than chaining uncertain star-formation scaling relations or sub-grid hydrodynamical prescriptions, the authors use an analytic halo model to directly calibrate a double power-law [C II] luminosity–halo mass relation, $L(M_h, z)$, solely against existing [C II] observations (tomographic cross-correlation intensity measurements at $0.4 < z < 4.2$ and ALMA/local luminosity functions at $z \simeq 0$ and $4.3 \lesssim z \lesssim 8$). By propagating the full posterior into the LIM power spectrum monopole, they provide empirical, data-driven error bars on the expected clustering and shot-noise signals to guide the design and forecasting of high-redshift [C II] experiments.

papers.title: Field-level inference under pressure: the information content of the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich field
papers.authors: Carmen Embil Villagra, Adrian E. Bayer, William R. Coulton, Alina Sabyr, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Blake D. Sherwin, Anthony Challinor, J. Colin Hill, Nicholas Battaglia
papers.abstract: The thermal Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (tSZ) field is highly non-Gaussian and contains cosmological information that cannot be fully captured by its angular power spectrum. In this work, we investigate the information content of this field using a convolutional neural network (CNN), and compare to simple and interpretable summary statistics, in a simulation-based inference (SBI) framework. We perform the first field-level analysis of the tSZ field, using a suite of $10{,}000$ simulated Compton-$y$ maps, where we jointly vary the cosmological parameters $\Omega_c$ and $\sigma_8$ (the density fraction for cold dark matter and the matter clustering amplitude, respectively) and two parameters describing the amplitude and shape of the electron pressure profile, $P_0$ and $\beta$, that aim to capture astrophysical uncertainties. We consider both noiseless simulations and simulations including realistic Simons Observatory (SO) noise after component separation. We use SBI to compare the constraints obtained from the CNN with those from the three Minkowski functionals (MFs), individually and in combination, as well as the angular power spectrum. This is the first application of SBI to the MFs of the tSZ field. We find that the CNN provides tighter constraints than conventional summary statistics in the noiseless case. However, at SO-like noise levels, the combination of MFs and the power spectrum recovers constraints comparable to those obtained with the CNN. Our results highlight the potential of these interpretable summary statistics, as well as field-level inference, for extracting information from the tSZ field, motivating efforts toward their application to real data.

conclusions: In the idealized noiseless case, the field-level CNN extracts significantly tighter constraints than conventional summary statistics, particularly improving on $\Omega_c$ and the outer pressure profile slope $\beta$.

When realistic Simons Observatory (SO) post-component-separation noise and Wiener filtering are included, combining the three Minkowski functionals with the angular power spectrum ($C_\ell^{yy}$) recovers essentially the same constraining power on $(\Omega_c, \sigma_8, P_0, \beta)$ as the full field-level CNN.

Using simulation-based inference (SBI) avoids assuming a Gaussian likelihood for highly non-Gaussian topological descriptors like Minkowski functionals, demonstrating that interpretable summary statistics can nearly saturate the information content of upcoming noisy tSZ maps without requiring direct pixel-level neural network application on real data.

Key caveats for real-data application include that the training maps used Poisson-sampled halos (neglecting halo clustering), spherical gas pressure profiles, and Gaussian uncorrelated foreground residuals rather than non-Gaussian correlated Cosmic Infrared Background (CIB) contamination.
ai.relevance_reason: Uses simulation-based inference and field-level vs. summary-statistic comparisons for late-time structure growth ($\sigma_8, \Omega_c$), which is loosely related to your interest in SBI and non-linear LSS observables, though focused on CMB secondary anisotropies (tSZ) rather than galaxy surveys or beyond-$\Lambda$CDM gravity.
ai.summary: The thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect—a spectral distortion of the CMB caused by photons inverse-Compton scattering off hot electrons in galaxy groups and clusters—traces the integrated line-of-sight electron pressure (the Compton-$y$ parameter) and is highly sensitive to late-time structure growth ($\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_c$). Because the tSZ field is dominated by collapsed halos, it is strongly non-Gaussian, meaning standard two-point statistics like the angular power spectrum ($C_\ell^{yy}$) miss much of its cosmological information. The authors generate 10,000 halo-model Compton-$y$ maps (varying $\Omega_c$, $\sigma_8$, and two intracluster gas pressure profile parameters $P_0$ and $\beta$) and use simulation-based inference (SBI) to benchmark a field-level convolutional neural network (ResNet-18) against interpretable summary statistics: $C_\ell^{yy}$ and the three Minkowski functionals ($V_0, V_1, V_2$, which measure the area fraction, boundary length, and topological genus of excursion sets above a threshold). This matters because it establishes how much total cosmological information exists at the field level in tSZ maps while marginalizing over gastrophysics, and tests whether simpler morphological statistics can capture that information under realistic Simons Observatory (SO) noise levels.

papers.title: Circular Axion String Loop Simulations: Field Theory and Effective Description
papers.authors: Mathieu Kaltschmidt, Javier Redondo, Ivan Rybak, Kenichi Saikawa, Iker Sanz-González
papers.abstract: An accurate description of axion strings and their radiation is crucial for understanding their cosmological implications. Motivated by the differing conclusions of previous works, we study a simple, controlled setup: the collapse of an initially static circular loop in a Minkowski background. We compare field-theory simulations of the conventional complex scalar and high-tension Klaer--Moore models with solutions of the renormalised Nambu--Goto--Kalb--Ramond (NGKR) equation of motion, covering the range $3 \lesssim \mathcal{T} \lesssim 100$ in dimensionless string tension. Both the field theory and NGKR approach the Nambu--Goto (NG) limit with corrections scaling as $1/\mathcal{T}$. However, the leading correction to the halving-time is $20-35\%$ larger in NGKR than in the field-theory simulations over the same range of tensions, while for large tensions the value agrees with an independent perturbative calculation to $0.2\%$. The late-time axion spectrum agrees with NGKR in the infrared, but the collapse generates additional structure in the ultraviolet part of the spectrum, which we attribute to different events such as an outgoing wave front that carries a sizable fraction of the energy or the rebound of the initial loop. These results provide a useful benchmark for a more accurate understanding of axion radiation from cosmological string networks.

conclusions: As dimensionless string tension $\mathcal{T}$ increases ($3 \lesssim \mathcal{T} \lesssim 100$), both standard complex scalar and Klaer–Moore field-theory simulations converge toward the thin-string Nambu–Goto limit with $1/\mathcal{T}$ corrections, validating the Klaer–Moore approach for accessing physical tensions around $\mathcal{T} \approx 70$.

The effective Nambu–Goto–Kalb–Ramond (NGKR) theory predicts slightly faster loop collapse than full field-theory simulations, with the leading $1/\mathcal{T}$ correction to the radius-halving time being $20\text{--}36\%$ larger in NGKR (though NGKR matches independent perturbative calculations at large $\mathcal{T}$ to $0.2\%$).
The radiated axion energy spectrum matches NGKR predictions at low wavenumbers (infrared peak and $1/k$ power law), which stems from the adiabatic contraction of the loop's initial self-field.

During the final nonlinear collapse ("focus") and core rebound, the loop emits an outgoing wave front that creates a flat plateau in the ultraviolet spectrum up to the core scale $k \approx m_s$, challenging the simple single power-law ($\propto k^{-q}$) spectral ansatz often assumed in cosmological network extrapolations.
ai.summary: If the symmetry responsible for the QCD axion (a leading cold dark matter candidate) breaks after inflation, it forms a cosmic network of topological defects called global axion strings, which decay by radiating axion particles. Predicting the resulting dark matter abundance—and thus the axion mass—requires knowing the energy spectrum of these radiated axions, but large-scale string network simulations currently disagree on whether the spectrum is dominated by low-energy (infrared) or high-energy (ultraviolet) modes, leading to an order-of-magnitude uncertainty in the predicted axion mass. Rather than simulating an entire tangled network, the authors isolate a single, initially static circular string loop in flat Minkowski space to benchmark full lattice field-theory simulations (using 3D uniform grids, 3D adaptive mesh refinement, 2D axisymmetric grids, and the high-tension Klaer–Moore two-scalar model) against the analytical Nambu–Goto–Kalb–Ramond (NGKR) effective theory for infinitely thin strings coupled to a long-range axion field. Covering dimensionless string tensions $3 \lesssim \mathcal{T} \lesssim 100$ (reaching the cosmologically relevant regime $\mathcal{T} \approx 70$), this controlled comparison tests how well effective thin-string approximations capture nonlinear collapse and radiation dynamics.

papers.title: Primordial Gravitational Waves in Loop Quantum Cosmology: Regularization Ambiguities and Initial State Dependence
papers.authors: Mah Noor Jamil, Parampreet Singh
papers.abstract: We compute the primordial tensor power spectrum in standard loop quantum cosmology and in the modified models mLQC-I and mLQC-II, evolving the tensor perturbations across the bounce in the hybrid and dressed metric prescriptions with a Starobinsky potential. In mLQC-I, the emergent de Sitter contracting branch requires the use of dedicated initial states. We use de Sitter mode function in the dressed metric approach and a Hankel-function solution in the hybrid approach. For inflationary e-foldings $N_e = 60$ and $65$, the pivot-scale tensor-to-scalar ratio agrees with the value of standard inflation with this potential. The scale-dependent ratio $r(k)=\mathcal{P}_T/\mathcal{P}_S$ cancels effects common to the two sectors and separates features that are independent of the initial state from those that depend on it. It varies slowly in the scale-invariant regime and oscillates around $r_\star$ at smaller $k$. The oscillations next to the scale-invariant regime do not depend on the adiabatic order, unlike the peaks and spikes at lower $k$. For a given initial state, the regularization dependence survives in the infrared, where long-wavelength modes retain a record of the bounce and of the pre-bounce branch. We propagate the normalized spectra to the CMB $B$-mode spectrum and discuss observational prospects.

conclusions: At the observational pivot scale (for $N_e = 60$ and $65$ e-folds of Starobinsky inflation), all three LQC regularizations and both perturbation prescriptions recover the standard slow-roll inflationary limit with $A_T \simeq 9.02 \times 10^{-12}$ and a tensor-to-scalar ratio $r_\star \simeq 4.3 \times 10^{-3}$—well below current bounds ($r < 0.036$) and within reach of LiteBIRD's target sensitivity ($\delta r < 10^{-3}$).

At intermediate and large scales (low $k$), the scale-dependent ratio $r(k) = \mathcal{P}_T(k)/\mathcal{P}_S(k)$ cancels common normalization effects and isolates physical bounce signatures—such as oscillations around $r_\star$ by a factor of a few—from unphysical sharp spikes caused by higher-order (2nd and 4th order) adiabatic initial-state approximations breaking down.

In the asymmetric mLQC-I model, which features an emergent Planckian de Sitter contracting phase, a Planck-scale infrared plateau appears in the dressed metric approach (using a de Sitter initial state) but vanishes in the hybrid approach (using a Hankel-function state), showing it is state- and prescription-dependent rather than a generic prediction of mLQC-I.

Propagating the spectra to the CMB $B$-mode angular power spectrum $C_\ell^{BB}$ shows that deviations from standard $\Lambda$CDM are restricted to the largest angular scales ($\ell \lesssim 20$, with mLQC-II deviating the most and mLQC-I the least), where cosmic variance and foregrounds make distinguishing between LQC regularizations via $B$-mode power spectra alone unlikely.
ai.summary: In loop quantum cosmology (LQC), the classical Big Bang singularity is replaced by a quantum bounce at Planckian energy densities, which can leave imprints on the largest observable scales of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) before standard slow-roll inflation takes over. However, predicting these signatures is complicated by three theoretical ambiguities: how the quantum Hamiltonian is regularized (giving standard LQC and two modified variants, mLQC-I and mLQC-II), how perturbations are quantized on the bouncing background (the "dressed metric" vs. "hybrid" prescriptions, which yield different effective masses near the bounce), and how the pre-bounce initial quantum vacuum state is chosen. The authors systematically evolve primordial gravitational waves (tensor modes) across the bounce under a Starobinsky inflationary potential across all combinations of these three models and two prescriptions, using dedicated non-adiabatic initial states for mLQC-I's asymmetric de Sitter contracting branch. By computing the primordial tensor power spectrum $\mathcal{P}_T(k)$, the scale-dependent tensor-to-scalar ratio $r(k)$, and the resulting CMB $B$-mode polarization spectrum $C_\ell^{BB}$, they disentangle genuine physical imprints of the quantum bounce from artifacts of the initial-state choice and quantization scheme.

papers.title: The Carousel Lens III: Joint lens convergence and source kinematic modeling
papers.authors: William Sheu, Xiaosheng Huang, Tania M. Barone, Fuyan Bian, Aleksandar Cikota, Karl Glazebrook, Tesla Jeltema, Evan Odell, Jackson H. O'Donnell, Linus Upson, Felipe Urcelay, Sean Xu
papers.abstract: We introduce a new, independent modeling component to the Carousel Lens series by exploiting the spatially-resolved kinematics contained within the lensed arcs, which so far has remained rather underexplored in strong-lensing analyses. We present an end-to-end forward-modeling framework that reconstructs an integral-field spectroscopic datacube from a parameterization of the lens convergence profile together with the line-of-sight velocity, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness profiles of the unlensed source. The kinematic structure of the source acts as an additional set of ray-traceable markers distributed across every lensed image, inaccessible from imaging data alone. Furthermore, by generating an [OII] emission-line datacube, we isolate a single source redshift and remove lens and line-of-sight light contamination. We apply this framework to deep VLT/MUSE observations of the Carousel Lens, modeling the [OII] emission of the quadruply-imaged star-forming galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ that anchors the system's cosmography constraints. We measure an Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and a logarithmic slope $\gamma = 1.412^{+0.002}_{-0.002}$, tightening the statistical uncertainties on both by roughly a factor of $2-2.5$ relative to the corresponding flat emission-line map model. We find that the source galaxy exhibits a strong rotation, lies confidently along the star-forming main sequence, and has an inferred central black hole mass of $\log M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot} = 7.89 \pm 0.51$. These results establish datacube-level forward modeling as a practical and independent route to traditional image-based lens models in the current systematics-limited regime, and one that extends naturally to this system's other lensed sources and to other lens systems.

conclusions: By jointly fitting the 3D spectroscopic datacube rather than a flat 2D emission-line image, the authors measure the lens's Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and logarithmic mass slope $\gamma = 1.412 \pm 0.002$, tightening statistical uncertainties by a factor of $\sim 1.8\text{--}2.5$ over comparable 2D image-only models.

Isolating the [O II] emission line removes foreground cluster light and reveals a demagnified central image near the cluster core, which probes smaller radii than previous Hubble imaging models and drives the shallower inferred inner mass profile slope ($\gamma \approx 1.41$ vs. $1.57\text{--}1.67$ at larger radii).

The reconstructed source galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ is a rapidly rotating disk galaxy with an asymptotic rotation velocity of $A_v = 266.2^{+11.3}_{-9.9}\text{ km s}^{-1}$, a central bulge velocity dispersion of $A_\sigma = 132.3^{+38.7}_{-31.1}\text{ km s}^{-1}$, and a turbulent gas dispersion floor of $C_\sigma = 37.16 \pm 0.38\text{ km s}^{-1}$.

From the source's kinematic and emission properties, they infer a dynamical mass of $\log(M_{\rm dyn}/M_\odot) = 10.35^{+0.15}_{-0.10}$, a star formation rate of $15.1 \pm 3.8\ M_\odot\text{ yr}^{-1}$ (placing it squarely on the star-forming main sequence), and a central supermassive black hole mass of $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot) = 7.89 \pm 0.51$.
