ai.summary: In strong gravitational lensing, precise models of the foreground lens's mass distribution are essential for cosmography—such as constraining $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and the dark energy equation of state $w$ from systems with multiple background sources at different redshifts—and are typically built using 2D images of the lensed arcs. However, integral-field unit (IFU) spectrographs record a full spectrum at every spatial pixel (producing a 3D "datacube" of two spatial dimensions plus wavelength), capturing Doppler shifts across the lensed arcs caused by the internal rotation of the background source galaxy. Because gravitational lensing does not alter wavelengths, parts of the source moving at a specific velocity must map to the exact same velocity in every multiple image, acting as an extra set of ray-traceable markers. The authors introduce a forward-modeling pipeline (`IFUL`) that simultaneously fits the foreground cluster's mass profile and the unlensed source's brightness, rotation velocity, and velocity dispersion profiles directly to a VLT/MUSE 3D datacube of the "Carousel Lens" ($z_{\rm l} = 0.488$), focusing on the [O II] emission doublet of a quadruply-imaged galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$. This approach strips away foreground lens light contamination to expose a faint central image near the cluster core and cuts statistical uncertainties on the lens mass parameters in half compared to 2D imaging alone, offering an independent cross-check for systematics-limited strong lensing cosmology.

papers.title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
papers.authors: Roland M. Crocker, Mark R. Krumholz
papers.abstract: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.

conclusions: Observational and dynamical constraints are jointly satisfied for moderate CGM cosmic-ray diffusion rates ($\mathcal{K} \simeq 0.05\text{--}0.2$, where $D_{\rm eff} = \mathcal{K}\,\tfrac{1}{3} r_{\rm vir} c_s$), corresponding to halo diffusion times comparable to the Hubble time.

In this slow-transport regime, roughly half of the cosmic-ray energy injected over an $L_\star$ halo's star-formation history remains in the CGM at $z \simeq 0$, providing dynamically significant pressure support without disrupting hydrostatic equilibrium.

With a CGM gas density slope of $\rho \propto r^{-\alpha}$ ($\alpha \simeq 1.8\text{--}2.9$), hadronic collisions from star-forming galaxies can account for 100% of the isotropic $\gamma$-ray background (~60% from extragalactic discs, 10–16% from extragalactic CGMs, and 24–28% from the Milky Way's own CGM).

In the same parameter space and without fine-tuning, non-radiative cosmic-ray streaming losses naturally supply the $\sim 5.5 \times 10^{39}\text{ erg s}^{-1}$ thermal heating required to match stacked eROSITA X-ray luminosities of $L_\star$ halos ($M_{\rm h} = 10^{12}\,M_\odot$).

A fast-diffusion scenario ($\mathcal{K} \gtrsim 1$) where cosmic rays escape freely into the intergalactic medium is also allowed by the bounds, but leaves cosmic rays dynamically negligible and requires an independent source to supply the remaining ~40% of the isotropic $\gamma$-ray background.
ai.summary: In normal star-forming galaxies, roughly 90% of relativistic protons—known as cosmic rays (CRs)—escape the dense galactic disc into the surrounding halo of diffuse gas called the circumgalactic medium (CGM), where their subsequent transport and dynamical impact are poorly understood. Because direct $\gamma$-ray detections of halo CRs are scarce and suffer from degeneracies between CR density and gas density, the authors construct a time-dependent semi-analytic model tracking halo growth, star-formation-driven CR injection, and CR propagation across cosmic time. They confront this model with five complementary bounds: the all-sky isotropic $\gamma$-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray luminosities from eROSITA (which bound non-radiative CR heating), outer Milky Way $\gamma$-ray emissivity from Fermi-LAT, and the dynamical requirements that CR pressure neither unbind the hydrostatic CGM nor disrupt virial shocks. They find that these constraints restrict viable models to either fast escape into the intergalactic medium or slow diffusion on Hubble timescales, arguing that the latter naturally explains both the IGRB and the thermal X-ray emission of $L_\star$ galaxy halos without invoking extra background sources.

papers.title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry
papers.authors: Ryota Takaku, Hiroaki Imada, Guillaume Patanchon, Yuki Sakurai
papers.abstract: Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.

conclusions: The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization ($4f_{\mathrm{HWP}}$) across CMB frequency bands (40–140 GHz) has an amplitude of order $10^{-4}$, a level small enough to be mitigated during map-making if properly modeled in the time-ordered data.
Unintended cross-polarization mixing between linear Stokes parameters ($Q$ and $U$) is negligible, inducing a spurious polarization-angle rotation of at most $\sim 30$ arcsec.

Varying the geometric asymmetry of the SWS across three idealized models yields no substantial differences in transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental polarization, though designs that enhance retardance allow thinner sapphire plates (useful for mass-limited space missions).

Comparing an actually fabricated SWS geometry with an idealized model reveals that higher overall transmittance ($M_{II}^{(0)}$) correlates with lower instrumental polarization, indicating that maximizing total transmission is more important for reducing systematics than fine-tuning SWS asymmetry.
ai.summary: To detect the tiny primordial $B$-mode polarization signal from inflation in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), telescopes often use a rotating half-wave plate (HWP)—an optical element that continuously rotates the polarization angle of incoming light so a single detector can measure polarization without suffering from low-frequency detector drift ($1/f$ noise). Because sapphire HWPs have a high refractive index, their surfaces are laser-etched with microscopic pyramids called anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) to prevent reflections without risking peeling at cryogenic temperatures; however, optical imperfections in the HWP and SWS can still convert unpolarized temperature fluctuations into fake polarization signals ("instrumental polarization") at four times the HWP rotation frequency ($4f_{\mathrm{HWP}}$), mimicking true sky polarization. In this paper, the authors use rigorous coupled-wave analysis (an electromagnetic solver for periodic gratings) to compute the full frequency- and angle-dependent Mueller matrices for a 5-layer LiteBIRD-like sapphire HWP across three idealized asymmetric SWS geometries as well as a realistic fabricated SWS profile. This characterization demonstrates that HWP-induced instrumental polarization is well within levels that can be corrected in map-making, and guides optical engineers to prioritize total transmission over structural asymmetry when fabricating future CMB polarimeters.

papers.title: The Influence of Hubble Expansion on the Future Merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda
papers.authors: Yufan Zhou, Tianchi Zhang, Shihong Liao, Zhiyuan Li, Lan Wang, David Benisty
papers.abstract: Most existing idealized simulations of galaxy mergers neglect Hubble expansion, as the local Hubble flow is curved by overdensities and the expansion effect is weak at these scales. However, even in the gravity-dominated Local Group (LG), the expansion itself still persists, and it has been shown important in some LG-related studies. Here we take the future merger of the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) as a case study to investigate the differences between simulations with and without Hubble expansion. We perform a suite of idealized N-body simulations of the MW--M31 system under pure Newtonian, $\Lambda$CDM, and $w_0w_a$CDM scenarios, testing different masses and proper motions of galaxies informed by current observational constraints. At low M31 tangential velocities, especially in cases where the two galaxies merge within a Hubble time, the expansion effect is negligible; while at high velocities (>66.5 km/s), the $\Lambda$CDM simulations introduce a noticeable delay in the merger time compared to the Newtonian ones and may even alter the final fate of the system, but the caveat here is that the isolated-pair idealization and the assumed expansion history break down. The delay is also present but less pronounced in the $w_0w_a$CDM runs. When M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud are included, the differences in merger times are reduced. In summary, Hubble expansion can play a noticeable role for galaxy mergers with high tangential velocities, but its actual influence on the MW--M31 merger depends on the precise masses and proper motions to be determined in the future.

conclusions: At low and intermediate M31 tangential velocities ($\lesssim 45\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$), cosmic expansion has a negligible effect ($\Delta t \lesssim 0.3\,\mathrm{Gyr}$, within the numerical noise floor), and can even slightly speed up the merger when a delayed first pericenter passage increases orbital energy loss from dynamical friction.

At high tangential velocities ($\ge 66.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$), the larger post-pericenter apocenter ($\sim 500\text{--}800\,\mathrm{kpc}$) exposes the galaxies to a significant dark energy repulsion relative to gravity (up to $\sim 18\%$ of the gravitational force), delaying the $\Lambda$CDM merger by $\ge 1\,\mathrm{Gyr}$ or preventing the merger entirely in low-mass configurations as the pair approaches the de Sitter radius ($r_\Lambda \sim 1.4\,\mathrm{Mpc}$).

In the DESI DR2-motivated $w_0w_a$CDM cosmology ($w_0 = -0.752, w_a = -0.86$), merger delays are smaller than in $\Lambda$CDM and unbound escapes do not occur, because the parameterized equation of state $w(a)$ crosses zero into the future ($a \sim 1.87$), shutting off dark energy acceleration.

Adding the massive satellites M33 and the LMC shrinks the first pericenter distance and speeds up the overall merger, which suppresses the impact of cosmic expansion and reduces the differences between Newtonian and expanding-background runs.

ai.summary: Idealized N-body simulations of galaxy mergers—such as the future collision between the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31)—almost always use pure Newtonian gravity in non-expanding space, assuming that the Local Group is completely decoupled from the cosmic expansion. However, when transforming from comoving coordinates with vacuum boundary conditions to physical coordinates, the background matter density cancels out of the equations of motion, leaving behind a repulsive dark energy acceleration ($\propto \Omega_\Lambda H_0^2 \mathbf{r}$ in $\Lambda$CDM) that grows linearly with separation and can affect wide orbits. To test whether this background expansion alters the fate of the Local Group, the authors run 108 idealized `GADGET-4` N-body simulations spanning observational uncertainties in MW/M31 halo masses and Gaia-derived proper motions, comparing pure Newtonian gravity against both standard $\Lambda$CDM and DESI DR2-motivated dynamical dark energy ($w_0w_a$CDM) expansion histories. This provides a clear physical test of when cosmological dark energy repulsion becomes dynamically relevant on sub-megaparsec scales and how sensitive local orbital predictions are to the assumed background cosmology and satellite galaxies (M33 and the LMC).

papers.title: Inelastic Kinetic Decoupling in WIMP Leptogenesis: A Minimal $Z_4$ Model
papers.authors: An Liu, Hong-Hao Zhang
papers.abstract: We study a minimal $Z_4$-symmetric extension of the Standard Model in which a singlet Dirac fermion $\chi$ constitutes dark matter, whose annihilations generate a lepton asymmetry through WIMP leptogenesis. Kinetic equilibrium is maintained mainly by the inelastic conversion $\chi L\leftrightarrow\bar\chi\Psi$. Compared with the near elastic regime, a sizable mass gap suppresses the conversion rate more rapidly as the Universe cools. This naturally drives kinetic decoupling to earlier times, even away from resonance. Starting from the full inelastic collision operator, we derive an effective momentum transfer rate for kinetic decoupling. We then solve the coupled Boltzmann equations for the dark matter abundance, its temperature $T_\chi$, and the $B-L$ asymmetry. Early kinetic decoupling can significantly modify the relic abundance, although near resonance this modification can be reduced by annihilation-induced heating. The $B-L$ asymmetry can be affected when asymmetry production overlaps with a substantial departure from kinetic equilibrium. In our scan, the largest deviations occur mainly for $x_{\rm lep}\gtrsim x_{\rm cd}$. After imposing our constraints, asymmetry production typically ends before chemical decoupling, leaving the final asymmetry essentially unchanged. For indirect detection, we generate the photon spectrum with Pythia and evaluate the Fermi-LAT dwarf spheroidal likelihood.

conclusions: Because the inelastic scattering process $\chi L \leftrightarrow \bar{\chi}\Psi$ requires producing the heavier fermion $\Psi$, it becomes exponentially (Boltzmann) suppressed as the universe cools, driving kinetic decoupling ($x_{\rm kd}$) to occur prior to chemical freeze-out ($x_{\rm cd}$) across the viable parameter space.

Early kinetic decoupling ($T_\chi \neq T$) significantly shifts the final dark matter relic abundance compared to standard equilibrium calculations whenever the annihilation cross section is velocity-dependent or near a mediator resonance, though annihilation-induced heating partially softens this effect near resonance.

In viable parameter regions where leptogenesis finishes before chemical freeze-out ($x_{\rm lep} < x_{\rm cd}$), the final $B-L$ baryon asymmetry is essentially insensitive to early kinetic decoupling; however, in excluded parameter regions where asymmetry generation extends past freeze-out ($x_{\rm lep} > x_{\rm cd}$), tracking $T_\chi$ can alter the final asymmetry by up to a factor of $\sim 1.97$.

The surviving parameter space that simultaneously reproduces the observed dark matter relic density ($\Omega_{\rm DM} h^2 \simeq 0.12$) and baryon asymmetry ($\eta_B \simeq 6.1 \times 10^{-10}$) remains fully consistent with indirect-detection gamma-ray limits from Fermi-LAT observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
ai.summary: In the early universe, "WIMP leptogenesis" models aim to solve two cosmic puzzles at once: dark matter particles ($\chi$) annihilate to set their own relic abundance while simultaneously violating CP symmetry to generate a matter–antimatter asymmetry in leptons (which electroweak sphalerons later convert into baryons). Standard calculations assume dark matter stays at the same temperature as the cosmic plasma ($T_\chi = T$) until annihilation freezes out, but if momentum-exchanging collisions shut off early—a phenomenon called early kinetic decoupling—the dark matter cools at a different rate, altering its velocity-dependent annihilation rates. The authors investigate a minimal $\mathbb{Z}_4$-symmetric particle physics model where dark matter maintains thermal contact primarily through inelastic scattering with Standard Model leptons into a heavier partner fermion ($\chi L \leftrightarrow \bar{\chi}\Psi$), which naturally shuts off early due to the mass gap as the universe cools. By deriving the full inelastic collision operator (since large momentum transfers across the mass gap invalidate standard Fokker–Planck approximations) and solving coupled Boltzmann equations for the dark matter density, dark matter temperature $T_\chi$, and $B-L$ asymmetry, they show that early kinetic decoupling strongly impacts the dark matter relic density while leaving the final baryon asymmetry largely untouched in viable parameter space.

papers.title: Elliptic master integrals and the one-loop cosmological wavefunction
papers.authors: Amara McCune, Matthew D. Schwartz
papers.abstract: Loop corrections to the cosmological wavefunction involve similar integrals to those required for scattering amplitudes. For the one-loop triangle of a conformally coupled scalar, the master integrals are elliptic, and so the triangle wavefunction coefficient was expected to be elliptic as well. Using a bootstrap approach, we compute this triangle coefficient exactly and show that it is not: the elliptic periods cancel, and the flat-space wavefunction coefficient is a combination of dilogarithms. The cancellation occurs because the residue of the loop integrand on the elliptic sector is a flat-space amplitude, rational in the loop momentum. The one-loop box, by contrast, is not polylogarithmic, even with a single external leg at each site. Its threshold discontinuity involves elliptic integrals, which we also give in closed form. For regular-tetrahedron momenta the periods of a K3 surface enter its loop integrand.

conclusions: In the one-loop triangle wavefunction coefficient, the elliptic periods present in individual master integrals completely cancel out, yielding a closed-form polylogarithmic expression of transcendental weight two (a linear combination of dilogarithms).

This cancellation happens because the residue of the physical loop integrand on the elliptic sector reduces to a flat-space scattering amplitude, which is a rational function of the loop momentum where square roots of the edge energies cancel.

Furthermore, the integrand of the one-loop triangle cosmological correlator has no poles on the planes where the loop measure defines an elliptic curve, meaning elliptic curves do not enter the triangle correlator at the integrand level either.

In contrast, the one-loop box diagram ($N=4$ vertices) in $d=3$ dimensions genuinely leaves the space of polylogarithms: its single-site partial-energy residue involves two square roots defining an elliptic curve, and for regular-tetrahedron external momenta, the loop integrand incorporates periods of a K3 surface.
ai.summary: To predict the statistical properties of primordial density fluctuations from inflation, theorists compute the "wavefunction of the universe," whose perturbative expansion in Feynman-like diagrams encodes late-time cosmological correlators. While tree-level diagrams for conformally coupled scalars yield simple rational functions or polylogarithms (generalizations of logarithms like the dilogarithm $\mathrm{Li}_2$), loop-level calculations have suggested that much more complex elliptic integrals might appear already at the one-loop triangle diagram. The authors investigate this using a semi-numerical bootstrap approach (combining exact differential equations and symbol calculus with high-precision numerical integration via the LLM-assisted `BootLoops` toolkit) to compute the one-loop triangle and box wavefunction coefficients directly. They show that the basis of "master integrals" used in standard reductions can be misleadingly complex: in the physical sum for the triangle diagram, all elliptic pieces cancel out, whereas genuine elliptic and higher-dimensional algebraic varieties (K3 surfaces) only emerge in the four-vertex box diagram.

papers.title: Constructing likelihoods for a non-Gaussian gravitational-wave background
papers.authors: Tore Boybeyi, Vuk Mandic, Joseph Romano
papers.abstract: The stochastic gravitational-wave background from stellar-mass compact binaries is non-Gaussian since it is made up of a finite number of individual mergers. Over the years, several methods have been developed to search for this background beyond the standard cross-correlation statistic. We reformulate the data analysis problem for such astrophysical backgrounds in terms of the characteristic function of the data in multiple detectors, and show that the existing searches arise as different limiting cases. We also show that new searches can be constructed through different approximations of the characteristic function, which gives a concrete way to engineer suitable approximate sufficient statistics. To illustrate this framework in the context of a simple example, we use the formalism proposed here to analyze an exactly solvable toy model.

conclusions: Using a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation, the authors derive an exact master equation for the population-marginalized GWB likelihood in terms of the single-merger characteristic function $z(\eta;\Lambda)$ and the Poisson mean number of events per segment $\bar{N}$.

Standard and existing non-Gaussian GWB searches are unified as specific truncations of this master likelihood: expanding $z$ to quadratic order in auxiliary variables $\eta$ recovers the standard Gaussian cross-correlation search, whereas expanding to first order in $\bar{N}$ yields deterministic and stochastic mixture-model likelihoods.

Expanding $\bar{N}(z(\eta;\Lambda)-1)$ in a functional basis establishes a one-to-one mapping between approximations of the data-independent characteristic function and families of approximate sufficient statistics (such as higher-order cross-moments of the data).

Incorporating even a single higher-order statistic beyond standard two-point cross-correlation captures the intermittent nature of the signal, breaking the degeneracy between the merger rate $\bar{N}$ and the per-event strain power.
ai.summary: When searching for a stochastic gravitational-wave background (GWB)—the combined hum of many faint, unresolved gravitational-wave signals—standard analyses assume the signal is a continuous Gaussian random field, which is fully described by its two-point cross-correlation between detectors. However, the astrophysical background from stellar-mass binary black hole mergers is actually intermittent ("popcorn-like") and non-Gaussian because only a finite number of short-lived mergers occur in any given time segment. The authors reformulate the GWB data analysis problem by applying a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation to linearize the signal in the likelihood, allowing them to analytically marginalize over the Poisson-distributed number of mergers and their source parameters. This yields an exact master likelihood governed by a single, data-independent quantity: the characteristic function (the Fourier transform of the probability distribution) of a single merger's strain signal. This framework unifies existing Gaussian and non-Gaussian searches as simple limiting cases and provides a systematic recipe for constructing new, computationally tractable "sufficient statistics" that compress the data while retaining non-Gaussian information about the underlying binary population.

papers.title: Unifying stochastic and deterministic signals: a practical search for the intermittent binary black-hole background
papers.authors: Tore Boybeyi, Vuk Mandic, Joseph Romano
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, the Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA detectors have detected nearly 400 compact binary mergers, most of which are stellar-mass binary black-hole (BBH) mergers. Nevertheless, most mergers in the Universe are too weak to be individually detected at current sensitivity levels. Since a BBH merger in band is much shorter than the average time between successive mergers, the population of these subthreshold events gives rise to an intermittent background of gravitational waves (GWs). This GW background is guaranteed to exist, but it has not yet been detected with current stochastic or deterministic searches. Here we propose a fast and accurate likelihood-based search for this background, which unifies the standard model-agnostic cross-correlation search and a fully deterministic, template-based search in a single likelihood. Our search is based on a truncated likelihood ratio, which is fully marginalized over the extrinsic parameters of the individual mergers, and which represents the data in two detectors as an expansion in terms of approximate sufficient statistics. These statistics are higher-order cross-moments of the data, weighted by geometrical factors that generalize the standard overlap reduction function (ORF) used in cross-correlation searches. We show that almost all the Bayesian evidence and information on the BBH merger population comes from correlations between frequency bins induced by individual mergers and is captured in the higher-order generalized ORFs. Consequently, any likelihood function that does not take these inter-frequency correlations into account is necessarily suboptimal. We validate our search on one year of simulated Advanced LIGO data, and find that a catalog-informed analysis, which uses information from both the detected and unresolved mergers, can infer the peak of the redshift distribution of the population of BBH mergers.

conclusions: The marginalized likelihood ratio for a merger signal of matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio $\rho_{\rm mf}$ saturates at expansion order $n_{\max} \approx \rho_{\rm mf}^2 / 2$, meaning choosing $n_{\max} > 32$ captures virtually all information from subthreshold mergers below a typical detection threshold of $\rho_{\rm th} = 8$.

Tests with phase-randomized data demonstrate that almost all Bayesian evidence and population information come from phase correlations between different frequency bins (captured by higher-order moments $n \ge 2$), which standard first-order cross-correlation searches miss completely.

In one year of simulated Advanced LIGO O4 data, unresolved subthreshold mergers alone yield a decisive detection of the gravitational-wave background and contribute roughly one-third of the total statistical information on the binary black-hole population.

Combining resolved catalog detections with the unresolved background in a unified analysis breaks degeneracies to successfully infer the peak redshift of the binary black-hole merger rate history—a constraint neither dataset can achieve alone.
ai.summary: While gravitational-wave detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA have individually resolved nearly 400 compact binary mergers, the vast majority of binary black-hole (BBH) mergers in the Universe are too distant and faint to pass detection thresholds. Because these brief signals arrive much less frequently than their duration in the detector band, they create an "intermittent" (popcorn-like, non-Gaussian) background of gravitational waves that standard stochastic cross-correlation searches—which assume a continuous Gaussian signal and ignore phase correlations across frequencies—are suboptimal at detecting. To bridge the gap between cheap stochastic cross-correlations and computationally expensive template-based searches, the authors expand the single-merger likelihood ratio into a power series of higher-order cross-moments of the matched-filtered detector data, analytically marginalizing over sky position, inclination, polarization, and distance via pre-computed geometrical weights called generalized overlap reduction functions (GORFs). Validating this framework on a year of simulated LIGO O4 data, they show it is fast enough to analyze millions of data segments while retaining the coherent phase information needed to detect the subthreshold BBH background and constrain the cosmic merger rate history.

papers.title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
papers.authors: Christian Partmann, Rachel S. Somerville, Michaela Hirschmann, Antti Rantala, Natalia Lahén
papers.abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.

conclusions: Without nuclear star clusters (NSCs), $10^3$–$10^4\,M_\odot$ IMBHs stall at separations of $50$–$200\,\text{pc}$ and capture virtually no gas; with $10^6\,M_\odot$ NSCs, the clusters sink and merge within $\sim 508\,\text{Myr}$, rapidly forming a bound IMBH binary.

The deep gravitational potential of the NSCs promotes gas capture after the merger-induced starburst subsides, growing the two black holes from $10^3\,M_\odot$ to $1.1\times 10^5\,M_\odot$ and $4.1\times 10^4\,M_\odot$ (~10 times more growth than in an isolated galaxy) in brief, supernova-regulated episodes with an active duty cycle of only $\sim 10\%$.

Three-body scattering of mostly pre-existing NSC stars increases the binary eccentricity from $e=0.7$ to $0.96$ and drives the IMBHs to merge via gravitational waves at $t \sim 848\,\text{Myr}$ ($\sim 340\,\text{Myr}$ after cluster coalescence), generating a strong LISA signal with $\text{SNR} \sim 10^3$ at $z=1$ and $\sim 190$ at $z=15$.

Stellar scouring by the binary and a gravitational-wave recoil kick of $\sim 175\,\text{km s}^{-1}$ eject the merged black hole from the cluster (leaving it wandering in the galaxy outskirts) and puff up the remnant NSC from an effective radius of $\sim 3\,\text{pc}$ to $\sim 6\,\text{pc}$ with a flattened core and fast rotation ($\lambda_R \sim 0.45$).
ai.summary: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, $10^2$–$10^5\,M_\odot$) are thought to be the building blocks of supermassive black holes, but in low-mass dwarf galaxies they struggle to merge on their own because dynamical friction—the gravitational drag from surrounding matter—is too weak to pull them to the galactic center, and there are too few nearby stars to shrink their orbits via three-body gravitational slingshots ("stellar hardening"). This paper investigates whether embedding these black holes inside dense nuclear star clusters (NSCs, $\sim 10^6\,M_\odot$) solves both bottlenecks during a gas-rich dwarf galaxy merger. The authors run high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations of two colliding dwarf galaxies ($4\,M_\odot$ gas resolution, resolving individual stars and supernova feedback with the GRIFFIN model) coupled to the regularized post-Newtonian integrator KETJU, which tracks exact close-range gravitational encounters and gravitational-wave inspiral without artificial force softening. They show that the massive NSCs act as heavy carriers that rapidly sink and merge, deepening the central gravitational potential to feed gas onto the black holes and supplying a dense reservoir of stars that drives the IMBH binary to coalesce within a billion years.

papers.title: Are Black Hole and Cosmological Horizon Thermodynamics Necessarily Inequivalent?
papers.authors: Zachary J. Hoelscher
papers.abstract: It has recently been argued that cosmological horizon thermodynamics and black hole thermodynamics are generically inequivalent in any consistent, UV complete theory of quantum gravity, where it was suggested that this could be falsified by the identification of a counterexample. This conjecture was motivated in part by noting that cosmological horizons do not incorporate many of the convenient features found in the black holes described by string theory. In this work, we consider as a toy model a universe with a single non-rotating black hole and a positive cosmological constant. We work in the Nariai limit where the mass of the black hole is taken to its maximum possible value, and where we also assert that the quantum field theory living on this background is strictly parity invariant. In the semi-classical regime where we neglect instability of the exact Nariai equilibrium under quantum fluctuations, we find that the observer cannot readily distinguish the physics in the neighborhood of the black hole horizon from the physics in the neighborhood of the cosmological horizon. This does not prove that the two are generically equivalent in any universe, though it does suggest that they cannot be entirely unrelated in general. We propose that any consistent theory of quantum gravity that aims to describe black holes in a universe with a positive cosmological constant should provide a related microscopic origin for the leading semiclassical cosmological entropy and black hole entropy in the neighborhood of the particular limit considered here.

conclusions: In the Nariai limit ($\mathrm{dS}_2 \times S_2$ geometry), the black hole and cosmological horizons sit at $\rho = \pm r_0$ with identical areas, entropies, Hawking temperatures, and scalar field absorption coefficients.

Because the metric is invariant under $\rho \leftrightarrow -\rho$ reflection, an observer situated at the static equilibrium point between the two horizons cannot distinguish near-horizon physics at the black hole horizon from that at the cosmological horizon, provided the underlying quantum field theory is strictly parity-invariant (e.g., an $SU(3) \times U(1)$ gauge theory with $\theta = 0$ and no weak interactions).

Although the Nariai spacetime is unstable to quantum fluctuations that eventually trigger black hole evaporation, the existence of even an unstable point of exact thermodynamic equivalence refutes the strict version of the Thermodynamic Split Conjecture.

Any candidate UV-complete theory of quantum gravity in a $\Lambda > 0$ universe must therefore provide related microscopic origins for black hole and cosmological horizon entropies as the system approaches the Nariai limit.
ai.summary: In quantum gravity, it is an open question whether the thermodynamics of cosmological event horizons (like the de Sitter horizon driven by a positive cosmological constant $\Lambda$) share the same microscopic origin as black hole horizon thermodynamics—a disconnect recently formalized as the "Thermodynamic Split Conjecture," which claims the two are generically inequivalent. To test this conjecture, the author analyzes a toy-model universe containing a single non-rotating black hole in a $\Lambda > 0$ background (Schwarzschild–de Sitter spacetime) pushed to the "Nariai limit," where the black hole mass is increased to its maximum possible value so that the black hole and cosmological horizons approach one another while maintaining a finite proper separation ($\mathrm{dS}_2 \times S_2$ geometry). By placing an observer on a static trajectory balanced between the two horizons and assuming a strictly parity-invariant quantum field theory (such as a weakless universe without chiral $SU(2)$ interactions), the spacetime exhibits an exact spatial reflection symmetry ($\rho \to -\rho$) that exchanges the two horizons. Consequently, the observer cannot semi-classically distinguish between the black hole and cosmological horizons, demonstrating that their thermodynamic descriptions cannot be completely unrelated in a consistent UV-complete theory of quantum gravity.

papers.title: The Korean Space Telescope (KST): A Dedicated Space Observatory for the Dark Universe
papers.authors: M. James Jee, Ho Seong Hwang, Dongwook Lim, Minjin Kim, Myungshin Im, Sungwook E. Hong, Ho-Gyu Lee, Soung-Chul Yang, David Parkinson, Arman Shafieloo, Jun-Qian Jiang, Haeng Pal Heo, Dongok Ryu, Hagyong Kihm, Hyung Yun Noh, Wooyong Kang, Youngsun Kim
papers.abstract: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.

conclusions: **Aperture–Etendue Optimization**: For a diffraction-limited three-mirror anastigmat with fixed optical complexity, survey grasp ($E \propto D^{-1}$) decreases with mirror diameter $D$, creating an "efficiency cliff" for larger mirrors; weighing this against the resolution needed to deblend faint galaxies ($\theta_g \sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$) yields a peak science-usable galaxy survey rate at $D \approx 1.4\text{ m}$ ($E \approx 0.385\text{ m}^2\,\text{deg}^2$).

**Simultaneous Dual-Channel Capability**: KST achieves 1-hour $5\sigma$ extended-source ($0.3^{\prime\prime}$ galaxy) depths of $g=26.1, r=25.7, i=25.3, z=24.9$ AB mag alongside $R \sim 100$ NIR spectrophotometry to $\sim 22.5$ AB mag per resolution element, targeting a photometric-redshift accuracy of $\sigma_z/(1+z) \lesssim 0.01$ and a weak-lensing multiplicative shear calibration accuracy of $m < 10^{-3}$.

**Dark Energy & Modified Gravity Constraints**: By combining weak lensing, angular BAO, the Alcock–Paczyński test in the $1.5 < z < 3$ "redshift desert", and a dust-resistant NIR Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram, KST is projected to constrain the dark energy equation of state at its pivot redshift to $\sigma(w_p) \sim 0.03$ while breaking degeneracies between evolving dark energy ($w_0\text{--}w_a$) and modified gravity.

**Dark Matter & Dark Sirens**: Diffraction-limited optical+NIR strong/weak lensing and flux-ratio anomalies will probe starless subhalos and cluster cores to distinguish cold, warm, fuzzy, and self-interacting dark matter, while the deep NIR galaxy catalog will provide statistical host redshifts for gravitational-wave "dark sirens" to measure $H_0$ independently of the cosmic distance ladder.

This paper presents the mission concept and design rationale for the Korean Space Telescope (KST), a proposed 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory engineered to tackle dark energy, dark matter, and gravitational-wave "standard sirens" (mergers whose waveforms give direct luminosity distances) with a single payload. Using a dichroic beam splitter and detectors with fixed optical coatings and a linear variable filter (LVF—a filter whose transmission wavelength varies continuously across the detector, yielding slitless low-resolution $R \sim 100$ spectra for every source as the telescope scans, without any moving parts), KST simultaneously captures diffraction-limited optical imaging ($g, r, i, z$ with a $\sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$ PSF) and $1.1\text{--}1.8\,\mu\text{m}$ near-infrared (NIR) spectrophotometry over a $1^{\circ} \times 0.25^{\circ}$ field of view. Through a two-tiered "Wedding Cake" survey ($2{,}000\text{ deg}^2$ Wide and $10\text{ deg}^2$ cluster-targeted Deep), KST fills a key observational niche complementary to Euclid, Roman, and Rubin by providing repeated time-domain coverage, simultaneous optical+NIR color/spectral mapping, and deep NIR photometric redshifts out to $z \sim 2\text{--}3$.

papers.title: Looking for gravitational waves with orbital dynamics: GUEST mission and the $μ$Hz band of Gravitational Waves
papers.authors: Diego Blas
papers.abstract: `Adding colour'' to the gravitational-wave sky by probing unexplored frequency bands has the potential to unveil new and unexpected phenomena in the Universe. The microhertz band, between pulsar timing arrays and LISA, is a particularly attractive target: it should host the extension of the signal recently found by pulsar timing arrays (if it is generated by a family of sources of gravitational waves), and it may harbour signals from the early Universe, primordial black holes or dark matter. In these proceedings, we review how the orbits of gravitationally bound systems act as resonant detectors of microhertz gravitational waves and ultra-light dark matter. We then describe GUEST (Gravitational Universe Exploration with Satellite Tracking), a mission concept recently proposed to the ESA F-class call, consisting of two dense passive spheres covered with retroreflectors, placed in highly eccentric Earth orbits and tracked by a global laser-ranging network.

conclusions: In an ideal global-orbit fit (as opposed to standard 7-day geodesy arc resets), a 10-year GUEST mission can probe a stochastic GW background down to fractional energy densities of $\Omega_{\rm GW} \lesssim 10^{-9}$ around $10\,\mu\text{Hz}$, sensitive enough to detect the high-frequency continuation of the NANOGrav supermassive black-hole binary background and distinguish it from early-Universe phase transitions or cosmic strings.

For individual merging supermassive black-hole binaries with total masses $M_{\rm tot} \sim 10^8\text{--}10^9\,M_\odot$, the global-fit analysis extends the detection horizon out to redshift $z \sim 1$, compared to just a few Mpc when using traditional short-arc re-fitting.

Because ultra-light dark matter (ULDM) behaves as an oscillating background field that drives gravitational potentials at frequency $2m_{\rm DM}$, GUEST can resonantly probe previously unexplored ULDM masses in the range $m_{\rm DM} \sim 10^{-20}\text{--}10^{-19}\,\text{eV}$, as well as scalar-induced GWs associated with planetary-mass primordial black holes ($M_{\rm PBH} \sim 10^{-7}\text{--}10^{-4}\,M_\odot$).

The high eccentricity ($e_0 = 0.75$) and long period ($P \approx 33.8\,\text{h}$) yield a perigee precession measurement $\sim 30$ times more precise than LAGEOS, significantly tightening constraints on Yukawa fifth forces at interaction ranges of $\lambda \sim 10^6\text{--}10^8\,\text{m}$.
ai.summary: Gravitational-wave (GW) astronomy currently leaves a major observational gap in the microhertz ($\mu\text{Hz}$) frequency band, which sits between the nanohertz regime of pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) and the millihertz regime of the upcoming LISA space interferometer. Instead of measuring fleeting shifts in light travel time like a traditional laser interferometer, gravitationally bound orbits can act as resonant detectors: when a passing GW has a frequency that is an integer multiple of a binary's orbital frequency, its perturbations accumulate over time, causing shifts in the orbital phase (true anomaly) that grow quadratically with time ($t^2$). In these proceedings, the author presents the science case and design for GUEST (Gravitational Universe Exploration with Satellite Tracking), an ESA F-class mission concept consisting of two dense, passive spheres covered in retroreflectors placed in highly eccentric ($e=0.75$), 33.8-hour Earth orbits and tracked over 10 years by ground-based satellite and lunar laser-ranging stations. By modeling the full orbital trajectory globally rather than resetting orbital fits every week (as is standard in geodesy), GUEST can bridge the $\mu\text{Hz}$ gap to test whether the recent PTA signal comes from supermassive black-hole binaries or early-Universe physics, while simultaneously testing ultra-light dark matter and fifth forces.

papers.title: Diamonds in the sky: the shape of gravitational waves from cosmic string cusps
papers.authors: Pierre Auclair, Chams Gharib, Danièle Steer
papers.abstract: We carry an in-depth analysis of the gravitational wave (GW) emission of cosmic string cusps, going beyond the seminal work of Damour and Vilenkin. We identify two features that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been described in the literature: first the GWs emission from a cusp, at any given frequency, is not concentrated inside a cone but instead draws a diamond-like shape in the sky. Second, the emission is not maximal in the direction of the cusp velocity, but in two slightly offset directions. We explain these effects in detail, and illustrate them with simplified examples. Then, we study two limiting cases for which the overall radiated power is enhanced: when the diamond is stretched in a particular direction, and when higher order derivatives vanish at the cusp. We statistically estimate the importance of these effects in a population of odd-harmonic loops.

conclusions: At a fixed gravitational wave frequency $f$, the high-frequency beaming pattern of a cosmic string cusp forms a four-cusped diamond (astroid-like) region on the sky rather than an axisymmetric cone, arising from the independent third-order Taylor expansions of the left- and right-moving string modes.

The gravitational wave amplitude is not maximal directly along the cusp's velocity vector; instead, projection effects cause the emission to vanish or dip at the exact center and peak in two slightly offset directions.

The total radiated GW power is significantly enhanced in two special limiting geometries: when one of the string modes has a small second derivative (stretching the diamond along one axis) or when the third derivative vanishes at the cusp (producing a flatter, stronger frequency spectrum than the standard $f^{-4/3}$ scaling).

Statistical analysis of random ensembles of odd-harmonic cosmic string loops shows how the distribution of loop shapes populates these geometric configurations, refining predictions for both individual GW burst searches and the stochastic gravitational wave background.
ai.summary: Cosmic strings are hypothetical one-dimensional topological defects—thin tubes of trapped energy left over from early-universe phase transitions—that form closed loops and oscillate relativistically, emitting bursts of gravitational waves (GWs). The strongest GW bursts come from "cusps," which are transient points along a string loop that briefly whip around at the speed of light and beam high-frequency radiation forward like a cosmic lighthouse. Revisiting the classic analytical calculation by Damour and Vilenkin, the authors carry out a detailed mathematical and statistical analysis of the angular radiation pattern and power emitted by cusps across ensembles of odd-harmonic string loops. They show that the standard textbook approximation of cusp emission as a simple circular cone is inaccurate, uncovering new geometric and directional structure that directly affects how GW detectors model burst waveforms and the stochastic gravitational wave background.

papers.title: Channelled versus Isotropic Accretion of Galaxy Groups onto Clusters: Kinematics, Spin Alignment, and Assembly Bias
papers.authors: Ankit Singh, Frazer Pearce, Meghan Gray, Ulrike Kuchner, Julian Onions, Gustavo Yepes, Alexander Knebe
papers.abstract: Galaxy clusters grow by accreting groups from the cosmic web, but whether the route of infall (along a cluster-connected filament or from the open field) imprints a group's kinematics, spin, and orbit remains unmeasured at scale. We classify $212{,}704$ group-cluster infall pairs across $27{,}029$ clusters in the $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 simulation into primary (cluster-connected), secondary (tributary), primary-outskirt, and isotropic channels using DisPerSE filaments. (i) In both channelled classes, group spin axes lie mainly parallel to the filament below a `spin-flip' mass and perpendicular above it, $\log_{10} M_\mathrm{flip}\;[h^{-1}\,M_{\odot}] = 13.07$ and $13.12$, a $0.05$-dex offset consistent with zero, lying $1.3-1.4$ dex above the field, while isotropic groups show no flip; $M_\mathrm{flip}$ stays radially flat out to $7\,R_{200}$. (ii) Within the primary class $M_\mathrm{flip}$ rises with the linear mass density of the host filament, from $12.96$ (thin tendrils) to $13.44$ (dense bridges); matching group mass, cluster mass and distance keeps the rise positive but leaves its size uncertain ($0.07-0.58$ dex). (iii) Isotropic groups fall below random alignment at $2\,R_{200}$ ($41$ per cent within $60^\circ$, a $4.3\sigma$ deficit). Primary groups show $85$ per cent velocity-filament alignment at $2\,R_{200}$, and isotropic groups infall $150-180\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ faster, and more radially, out to $5\,R_{200}$. At matched distance isotropic groups are therefore predicted to reach orbital pericentres up to $10$ per cent smaller than primary groups, whose smaller pooled pericentres reflect only their proximity to the cluster. The topological route of accretion, and within it the host filament's linear density, shapes how groups enter clusters, testable with wide-area spectroscopic surveys.

conclusions: **Filamentary spin-flip occurs at significantly higher halo masses**: Group spin axes transition from parallel to perpendicular alignment with their host filament at $\log_{10}(M_\mathrm{flip}/[h^{-1}M_\odot]) \approx 13.07$ (primary) and $13.12$ (secondary), which is $1.3\text{--}1.4\text{ dex}$ higher than in the field, while isotropic groups show no spin flip at all; physically, the intense, anisotropic tidal shear near clusters forces the parallel-to-perpendicular spin crossover to much more massive systems.

**Spin-flip mass scales with filament linear density**: Within primary filaments, $M_\mathrm{flip}$ increases by $0.49\text{ dex}$ from $10^{12.96}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$ in thin tendrils to $10^{13.44}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$ in dense bridges, confirming that local tidal environment and mass density govern angular momentum acquisition rather than mere network topology.

**Contrasting infall kinematics and velocity alignments**: Groups in primary filaments stream coherently along filament axes ($85\%$ aligned within $60^\circ$ at $2\,R_{200}$), whereas isotropic groups are mildly anti-aligned with nearby filaments (only $41.4\%$ within $60^\circ$, a $4.3\sigma$ deficit) and infall $150\text{--}180\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ faster and more radially.

**Orbital pericentres driven by distance, not channelling**: At matched cluster-centric distance, isotropic groups are predicted to reach pericentres up to $10\%$ smaller than filament groups due to their higher radial speeds; the smaller overall pericentres found for pooled filament groups simply reflect their closer proximity to the cluster.

**Signatures of assembly bias in halo concentration**: Groups accreting from the field exhibit slightly higher NFW concentrations at fixed mass than channelled groups, consistent with tidal starvation in underdense regions causing earlier halo formation.

ai.summary: As galaxy clusters grow at the nodes of the cosmic web, they accrete smaller galaxy groups either guided along dark matter filaments (channelled accretion) or directly from underdense field environments (isotropic accretion). According to tidal torque theory, local gravitational tides imprint on halo angular momentum, producing a "spin-flip" transition where low-mass halos spin parallel to their host filament while more massive halos, assembled by late mergers along the filament, spin perpendicularly. Analyzing over $210{,}000$ group–cluster infall pairs across $27{,}029$ clusters in the $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 $N$-body simulation, the authors used the topological filament finder DisPerSE to classify accretion into primary (cluster-feeding), secondary (tributary), and isotropic channels. They discovered that the group spin-flip mass in filaments sits over an order of magnitude higher than in the general field and systematically rises with the host filament's linear mass density, while isotropic groups infall faster, more radially, and with mild kinematic anti-alignment. These findings provide large-scale, quantitative predictions connecting cosmic web geometry to group kinematics and assembly bias, offering clear observational benchmarks for upcoming wide-area spectroscopic surveys.

papers.title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
papers.authors: Adrian E. Bayer, David N. Spergel
papers.abstract: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

conclusions: **Multivariate distributions catch blind spots of $\chi^2$:** Standard scalar summaries like $\chi^2$ or mean-difference tests (Hotelling's $T^2$) discard directional and higher-order shape information, whereas multivariate partition tests (like PQMass) successfully detect diverse systematics including calibration jitter, angular concentration, and correlated data splits.

**Coadding masks observation-level variation:** Averaging repeated observations into a deep coadded map before testing suppresses observation-to-observation fluctuations; in CMB $B$-mode simulations, ensemble testing reaches 50% detection at systematic amplitudes as low as 1/8th of those required by a conventional coadded $\chi^2$ test.

**Ensemble scaling behavior:** Detection power scales steeply with the number of observation units $N$ (PQMass detection rising from $\sim 15\text{--}30\%$ at $N=20$ to near saturation at $N=100\text{--}250$), and reference-ensemble requirements saturate around $N_{\rm ref} \approx N$ for partition-based tests.

**Broad applicability and localization:** Beyond CMB polarization systematics, the framework recovers broken velocity-reflection symmetry from Gaia DR3 moving groups nearly as sensitively as an informed matched filter, and localizes specific DNA-damage cellular sub-populations in CRISPR screens.

ai.summary: In observational cosmology, pipelines rely heavily on "null tests"—such as differencing data splits that observe the same patch of sky—to verify that instrument systematics do not masquerade as faint physical signals like primordial CMB $B$-mode polarization. Conventional pipelines typically average these repeated observations into a single coadded dataset and compress the result into a scalar $\chi^2$ statistic, which discards directional structure and erases observation-to-observation variability. To address this, the authors introduce an ensemble null-testing framework that directly compares multivariate distributions of un-coadded measurement vectors against reference distributions using non-parametric tools such as PQMass (which partitions multi-dimensional feature space). Demonstrating the method on CMB $B$-mode simulations with six injected systematics, Gaia DR3 stellar kinematics, and biological screens, they show that ensemble testing detects varying systematics at amplitudes up to eight times weaker than standard coadded $\chi^2$ tests while localizing which feature combinations drive the discrepancy.

papers.title: Celia: Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions
papers.authors: Xiaowen Zhang, Matthew Ho, Anshul Kumar, Tiziana Di Matteo, Rupert A. C. Croft, Barnabás Póczos
papers.abstract: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations connect observed galaxies to cosmology and the physics of galaxy formation. Each simulation is expensive, and different codes model galaxy formation in different ways. We present Celia (Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions), a self-supervised foundation model that maps catalogs of subhalos and their galaxy properties to an embedding vector for the purposes of compression and organization of astrophysical and large-scale structure information. Celia is pretrained without parameter labels on the IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites of CAMELS and their N-body counterparts, by reconstructing masked subhalo properties and predicting the representations of a teacher network. Simple linear models fitted to the embeddings recover $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$ with $R^2=0.999$, and $\sigma_8$ and both supernova-feedback amplitudes with $R^2\geq0.97$, in all three suites. The embeddings translate well to out-of-distribution simulations such as Swift-EAGLE, a code that Celia never saw. A linear model fitted on the three training codes predicts its $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$ with a correlation coefficient $r=0.985$, and linear models fitted on 20 labeled simulations reach $r\geq0.94$ for $\Omega_{\mathrm m}$, $\sigma_8$ and a supernova-feedback amplitude. We decompose the variation among the simulations of each suite into principal components of the embedding, and simple power laws of the simulation parameters describe the leading components. Celia gives simulated galaxy catalogs a shared coordinate system for simulation-based inference, emulation, the comparison of galaxy-formation models, the detection of physical degeneracies and the discovery of new astrophysical probes.

conclusions: Linear readouts on frozen embeddings accurately recover cosmology: Simple linear models achieve $R^2 = 0.999$ for $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$, $R^2 \in [0.986, 0.991]$ for $\sigma_8$, and $R^2 \geq 0.97$ for supernova feedback amplitudes across all three training suites, showing the self-supervised representation effectively preserves both large-scale structure and baryonic physics.

Zero-shot and few-shot transfer to unseen simulation codes: When evaluated on Swift-EAGLE without retraining the encoder, linear readouts trained on the other three codes predict $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ with correlation $r = 0.985$ ($R^2 = 0.825$), and fitting linear readouts with only 20 labeled simulations recovers $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\sigma_8$, and supernova feedback with $r \geq 0.94$.

Physical parameter decoupling from cosmic variance: The embedding separates physical parameter shifts from initial-condition scatter (cosmic variance) by factors of 4 to 59, ordering catalogs along interpretable directions where feedback parameters scaling similar physical mechanisms across different codes align.

Confidence calibration driven by catalog astrophysics: Prediction error estimates derived directly from the embeddings physically correlate with tracer populations—for example, confidence on kinetic AGN feedback parameters grows from $0.03$ to $0.84$ as the number of massive black holes driving that feedback rises from 0 to $\sim 75$.
